Deepest mines: **Mponeng, TauTona** (South Africa), only **3.9 km**.

6.s:
Consider the following statements:

I. Silicon and oxygen are common elements in all types of feldspar and sodium, potassium, calcium, aluminium etc. are found in specific feldspar variety.

II. Almost one-fourth of the Earth's crust is composed of feldspar and quartz.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
6.x: Statement I is NCERT verbatim on feldspar; but NCERT says half (not one-fourth) of the crust is feldspar, so Statement II is wrong – Statement I only.

6.s: Which one of the following is present in the largest amount in terms of per cent by mass in the Earth's crust?
6.x: Oxygen (46.6%) is the most abundant element in the crust by mass; silicon (27.7%) is second.

6.s: A chemical element found in abundance in the Earth’s crust is–
6.x: Oxygen (46.6%) is the most abundant element of the crust, ahead of silicon, aluminium and iron.

6.s: Which of the following elements are found in highest and lowest quantities respectively in the crust of the Earth?
6.x: Oxygen is the highest (46.6%); among the listed elements magnesium (2.1%) is the lowest, below sodium and calcium.

6.s: The most abundant element in Earth’s crust is
6.x: Oxygen makes up 46.6% of the crust, the highest; silicon is second at 27.7%.

6.s: The second-most abundant metal in earth's crust is:
6.src: APPSC Divisional Accounts Officer (Mains) General Studies &
6.x: Aluminium (8.1%) is the most abundant metal in the crust and iron (5.0%) is the second.

6.s: The element which is present in large amounts in rocks and minerals is
6.x: Silicon (27.7% of the crust) occurs as silica and silicates that form most rocks and minerals.

6.s: Among the following, the most abundant metal in the Earths crust is
6.x: Aluminium (8.1%) is the most abundant metal in the crust; iron (5.0%) is second.

6.s: Which of the following is not a form of Calcium Carbonate?
6.src: APPSC ASO Mains General Studies & Mental Ability 2017
6.x: Granite is a silicate igneous rock; limestone, chalk and marble are all calcium carbonate.

6.s: Identify a mineral from the phyllosilicate class.
6.src: APPSC Forest Range Officer Screening Test General Studies &
6.x: Muscovite (mica) is a sheet silicate – a phyllosilicate; albite is a tectosilicate, hornblende a double-chain and augite a single-chain inosilicate.

6.s: What is the term used for the process in which minerals crystallise from magma?
6.src: APPSC Forest Range Officer Screening Test General Studies &
6.x: Bowen's reaction series is the order in which minerals crystallise from cooling magma (olivine first, quartz last).

6.s: Chalk and marble are different forms of
6.x: Chalk and marble are both calcium carbonate (CaCO3) – chalk sedimentary, marble its metamorphic form.

6.s: The scale used to find out the hardness of mineral is:
6.x: The Mohs scale (talc 1 to diamond 10) measures the hardness of minerals; Mercalli and Rossi-Forel measure earthquake intensity and Beaufort wind force.

6.s: The scale used to find out the hardness of mineral is:
6.x: Mineral hardness is measured on the Mohs scale; Mercalli and Rossi-Forel are earthquake-intensity scales, Beaufort is wind.

6.s: Which is the second most abundant element by weight in the Earth's crust?
6.x: Oxygen is the most abundant element by weight in the crust, followed by silicon at about 27.72%.
xa: **Aluminium** is the **most abundant metal**; **iron** second.
⚠ JPSC **2011** keyed **Aluminium** for "second largest".
In the **whole Earth**, **iron** dominates (iron-rich core).

6.s: Which is the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust by weight?
6.x: Aluminium (about 8.1%) is the most abundant metal in the crust, followed by iron (about 5%) and calcium (about 3.6%). Silicon (about 27.7%) is more abundant but is not a metal; oxygen is the most abundant element overall.
6.tq: Element order O > Si > Al > Fe; most abundant metal = Al.
xs: **Aluminium** (**8.13%**) is the most abundant **metal** in the crust — option **(2)**.
**Iron** (**5.00%**) is second; **calcium** (**3.63%**) next.
**Silicon** (**27.72%**) is more abundant but not a metal.
xa: **Oxygen** (**46.60%**) is the most abundant element overall.
⚠ JPSC **2011** keyed **Aluminium** for "second largest".
In the **whole Earth**, **iron** dominates.

6.s: Which of the following statements about the composition of Earth’s crust is incorrect?
o: Aluminium constitutes 8.13% by weight and ranks third.
Silicon constitutes 27.72% by weight and ranks second.
Iron constitutes 8.13% by weight and ranks third.
Oxygen constitutes 46.60% by weight and ranks first.
6.x: Option C is incorrect: iron is about 5% and ranks fourth. Aluminium is third at 8.13%, after oxygen (46.60%) and silicon (27.72%).
6.tq: Check the rank and figure of each element.
n: Oxygen constitutes 46.60% of Earth’s crust by weight. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Oxygen ranks first among the elements in Earth’s crust by weight. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Silicon constitutes 27.72% of Earth’s crust by weight. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Silicon ranks second among the elements in Earth’s crust by weight. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Aluminium constitutes 8.13% of Earth’s crust by weight. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Aluminium ranks third among the elements in Earth’s crust by weight. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Iron constitutes 5.00% of Earth’s crust by weight. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Iron ranks fourth among the elements in Earth’s crust by weight. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xs: The incorrect statement is "**Iron constitutes 8.13% by weight and ranks third**" — option **(3)**: iron is **5.00%** and ranks **fourth**.
**8.13%** and **third rank** belong to **aluminium**.
The others are correct: **oxygen 46.60%** (first), **silicon 27.72%** (second).
xa: Then **calcium 3.63%**, **sodium 2.83%**, **potassium 2.59%**, **magnesium 2.09%**.
**Aluminium** is the **most abundant metal** in the crust; **iron** second.
⚠ JPSC **2011** keyed **Aluminium** for "second largest".
**Whole Earth:** **iron** dominates (core is iron-rich).

6.s: Oxygen makes up about what percentage of the Earth's crust by weight?
6.x: Oxygen, at 46.60%, is the most abundant element of the crust; silicon is 27.72%, aluminium 8.13% and iron 5%.

6.s: Which is the second-most abundant element in the Earth's crust by weight?
6.x: Silicon ranks second at about 27.7%; iron is the second-most abundant metal (~5.0%).
xa: Ranks 5–7: **Calcium 3.6**, **Sodium 2.8**, **Potassium 2.6**.
⚠ For the whole Earth, **magnesium (13.9%)** ranks fourth after iron, oxygen and silicon.

6.s: Which is the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust?
6.x: Aluminium (8.1%) is the most abundant metal in the crust; iron (5.0%) is second. Iron leads only for the whole Earth.

6.s: Which is the second-most abundant metal in the Earth's crust?
6.x: Iron, at 5.0% by weight, is the second-most abundant metal after aluminium (8.1%).

6.s: What is quartz, a major component of granite and sandstone, chemically?
6.x: Quartz is silicon dioxide (SiO2), hard and resistant to weathering, and a major component of granite and sandstone.
xa: Quartz is a **tectosilicate** (framework), like **albite** and **orthoclase**.
Quartz is the **most stable** mineral of Bowen's series; **olivine** forms first.

6.s: Feldspar makes up approximately what proportion of the Earth's crust?
6.x: Feldspar makes up approximately half of the Earth's crust; 'one-fourth' is incorrect.
xa: ⚠ APPSC G1 **2024** used this exact trap: "one-fourth" is wrong — answer was **statement I only**.
Feldspars (**albite, orthoclase**) are **tectosilicates** (framework silicates).
**Quartz** (**SiO2**) is hard, resists weathering and forms a major part of **granite and sandstone**.

6.s: Muscovite belongs to which silicate class?
6.x: Muscovite is a phyllosilicate; albite is a tectosilicate, hornblende a double-chain and augite a single-chain inosilicate.
xa: **Olivine** is a **nesosilicate** (isolated tetrahedra).
Tectosilicates (framework) include **albite, orthoclase** and **quartz**.
⚠ "Mica = **phyllosilicate**" was asked in **APPSC 2024**.

6.s: Which of the following pairs (mineral – position in Bowen's reaction series) is correctly matched?
o: Quartz – Crystallises last and is most stable
6.x: Quartz crystallises last from cooling magma and is the most stable mineral in Bowen's reaction series; olivine crystallises first.

6.s: In the discontinuous branch of Bowen's reaction series, which is the first mineral to crystallise?
6.x: The discontinuous branch runs olivine → pyroxene → amphibole → biotite; mafic minerals form first at the highest temperature.
xa: The series ends with **K-feldspar → muscovite → quartz**; **quartz is last** and most stable.
Bowen's series shows the order of **crystallisation from cooling magma** (APPSC **2024**).

6.s: Which mineral has a Mohs hardness of 7?
6.x: Quartz has a Mohs hardness of 7. Orthoclase is 6, topaz is 8 and apatite is 5.
6.tq: Use the central value in the hardness scale and distinguish neighbouring entries.
xs: **Quartz** has a Mohs hardness of **7** — option **(4)** is correct.
On the scale, **apatite** is 5, **orthoclase** 6 and **topaz** 8.
xa: The scale runs **1–10**: from **talc** (1) to **diamond (10)**; **corundum** sits just below diamond.
Quartz (**SiO2**) forms a major part of **granite and sandstone** and crystallises **last** in Bowen's series.

6.s: Hornblende belongs to which silicate class?
6.x: Hornblende (amphibole) is a double-chain inosilicate; augite is single chain and mica a phyllosilicate.

6.s: Which of the following pairs (mineral – Mohs hardness) is correctly matched?
6.x: On the Mohs scale topaz is 8; apatite is 5, orthoclase 6 and calcite 3.

6.s: Which is the softest mineral on the Mohs scale of hardness?
6.x: The Mohs scale runs from talc (1), the softest, to diamond (10), the hardest.

6.s: To which silicate class does augite (pyroxene) belong?
6.x: Augite, a pyroxene, is a single-chain inosilicate; hornblende is double-chain.

6.s: Feldspars such as albite and orthoclase belong to which silicate class?
6.x: Albite and orthoclase (feldspars) and quartz are framework silicates, called tectosilicates.

6.s: Basalt is an
6.src: APPSC Forest Beat Officer & Assistant Beat Officer General S
6.x: Basalt forms when lava cools fast on the surface – a fine-grained extrusive igneous rock.

6.s: Which of the following Rock is not a Igneous rock?
6.x: Quartzite is metamorphic (from sandstone); granite, basalt and pegmatite are igneous.

6.s: Which one of the following is not an igneous rock?
6.x: Dolomite is a sedimentary carbonate rock; gabbro, granite and basalt are igneous.

6.s: Granite and Basalt are the examples of which of the following?
6.x: Granite (intrusive) and basalt (extrusive) are both igneous rocks.

6.s: Which of the following rocks consist of large grained crystals?
6.x: Plutonic (intrusive) rocks cool slowly at depth and so have large crystals; extrusive rocks are fine-grained and shale and loess are sedimentary.

6.s: Granite is a/an:
6.x: Granite is coarse-grained and solidifies slowly beneath the surface – an intrusive igneous rock.

6.s: Which of the following rocks is not likely to contain fossils?
6.x: Granite, formed from magma, has no fossils; conglomerate, shale and sandstone are sedimentary and may hold fossils.

6.s: Which statement of the following is true for igneous rocks?
o: They are both crystal and non-crystal
6.x: Igneous rocks are both crystalline and non-crystalline; they have no fossils (not 'little'), are poorly porous and are made of silicates.

6.s: Which type of rock is formed from cooling and solidification of lava ?
6.x: Rocks formed by cooling and solidification of magma or lava are igneous.

6.s: Deccan Plateau is formed mainly from
6.src: APPSC Assistant Social, BC & Tribal Welfare Officers Screeni
6.x: The Deccan Plateau is formed mainly of igneous rock – the basalt lava flows of the Deccan Traps.

6.s: The Deccan Plateau is mostly composed of which type of rock?
6.src: APPSC Forest Beat Officer & Assistant Beat Officer (Mains) P
6.x: The Deccan Plateau is mostly basalt (Deccan Trap lava); granite, sandstone and limestone are minor.

6.s: Which type of rocks are predominant in Deccan Traps?
6.src: Civil Assistant Surgeon Vaidya Vidhana Parishad 2017
6.x: Basalt predominates in the Deccan Traps (fissure lava flows).

6.s: Major portion of Deccan Traps are made of
6.x: The Deccan Traps are made mainly of basalt; laterite is a soil and sandstone/limestone are sedimentary.

6.s: What is the approximate age of Deccan Plateau in million years (choose the nearest figure)?
6.src: APPSC Technical Assistant (Geo Physics) / Technical Assistan
6.x: The Deccan Traps erupted at the end of the Cretaceous, about 66 million years ago, so 65 is the nearest figure.

6.s: Which of the following is a coarse-grained intrusive igneous rock?
6.x: Intrusive rocks cool slowly at depth, forming coarse grains, as in granite and gabbro.
xa: **Extrusive (volcanic)** lava cools fast at the surface → **fine-grained**: **basalt, rhyolite, andesite**.
APPSC G2 **2024**: **granite = intrusive igneous**.
**Hypabyssal** rocks occur in **dykes and sills** — e.g. **dolerite**.

6.s: Which of the following is a felsic extrusive igneous rock?
6.x: Rhyolite is felsic extrusive; granite is felsic intrusive, diorite intermediate intrusive and basalt mafic extrusive.
xa: **Gabbro** is the **mafic intrusive** counterpart of basalt.
**Andesite** is another extrusive (volcanic) rock.
Volcanic rocks (**andesite, dacite, rhyolite, basalt**) need more energy to fracture than many sedimentary rocks.

6.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Felsic igneous rocks are generally light-coloured and silica-rich.
2. Mafic rocks are always less dense than felsic rocks.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
6.x: Felsic rocks are silica-rich, light-coloured and relatively low in density; mafic rocks, rich in iron, magnesium and calcium, are dark and dense, so statement 2 is wrong.
xa: ⚠ APPSC **2024** Assertion-Reason: "felsic rocks contain high iron, magnesium and calcium" is **false** — that describes **mafic** rocks.
Intrusive examples: felsic = **granite**; intermediate = **diorite**; mafic = **gabbro**.
Mafic minerals include **olivine** and **pyroxene**.

6.s: What are dark, dense igneous rocks rich in iron, magnesium and calcium called?
6.x: Mafic (basic) rocks are rich in Fe, Mg and Ca; felsic rocks are silica-rich and light-coloured.

6.s: Which type of rock is diorite?
6.x: Diorite is intermediate intrusive; rhyolite is felsic extrusive, granite felsic intrusive and basalt mafic extrusive.

6.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about rocks?
o: Igneous rocks form by cooling of magma or lava
Granite is extrusive igneous and basalt is intrusive igneous
Metamorphic rocks are existing rocks altered by heat or pressure
Sedimentary rocks form through surface deposition
6.x: It is the reverse: granite is intrusive igneous and basalt is extrusive igneous.
n: Igneous rocks form through cooling or solidification of magma or lava. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Sedimentary rocks form through surface deposition. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Metamorphic rocks form when existing rock is altered by heat or pressure. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Granite is an intrusive igneous rock. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Basalt is an extrusive igneous rock. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xa: Igneous rocks are "**primary**" rocks (APPSC **2019**) and hold **no fossils**.
**Sedimentary** examples: sandstone, limestone, shale, **coal**; **metamorphic**: marble, slate, quartzite, gneiss.
⚠ **Felsic** (granite) = silica-rich; **mafic** (gabbro) = rich in **iron, magnesium, calcium** (APPSC **2024** trap).
**Deccan Trap** basalt (~**65 million years**) gives **black cotton soil**.

6.s: The rocks in Himalayan Mountains are?
6.x: The Himalayas are folded sedimentary rocks of the Tethys Sea; granite is a rock, not a class, and igneous/metamorphic rocks are only in the core.

6.s: These rocks were used in the construction of Red Fort and Agra Fort in India.
6.x: The Red Fort and Agra Fort are built of red sandstone, a sedimentary rock.

6.s: Coal is an example of –
6.x: Coal is an organically formed sedimentary rock.

6.s: The rocks in the Himalayan system are primarily characterised as
6.x: The Himalayas are made primarily of sedimentary rocks (folded Tethys sediments); plutonic rock and dykes occur only locally.

6.s:
Consider the following statements made about the sedimentary rocks:
1. Sedimentary rocks are formed at Earth's surface by the hydrological system.
2. The formation of sedimentary rocks involves the weathering of pre-existing rocks.
3. Sedimentary rocks contain fossils.
4. Sedimentary rocks typically occur in layers. Which of these statements are correct?
6.x: All four are correct: sedimentary rocks form at the surface through the hydrological system, from weathering of older rocks, contain fossils and occur in layers.

6.s:
Consider the following statements:
1.
Statement I: In the context of effect of water on rocks, chalk is known as a very permeable rock whereas clay is known as quite an impermeable or least permeable rock.
2. Statement II: Chalk is porous and hence can absorb water.
3. Statement III: Clay is not at all porous. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements? Physical Geography PMF IAS Geo – 2
o: Both Statement II and Statement III are correct and both of them explain Statement I
Both Statement II and Statement III are correct but only one of them explains Statement I
Only one of the Statements II and III is correct and that explains Statement I
Neither Statement II nor Statement III is correct
6.x: Chalk is porous and so absorbs water (II correct, explains I); clay is porous but impermeable, so III ('not at all porous') is wrong.

6.s: Regarding sedimentary rocks which of the following statements is true?
o: These are such rocks whose structure depend on
These rocks are deposited in layers
These rocks cannot be formed in water
6.x: Sedimentary rocks are deposited in layers (strata); they are not crystalline and most form in water.

6.s: Sandstone is flaky rock, because –
o: It is formed in the desert
It is formed due to Heat
It is formed on the mountain
6.x: Sandstone is a layered (flaky) rock because its sand grains were deposited under water.

6.s: Preserved traces of living organisms retained in the form of impressions of the body parts in the soil are called ............. .
6.x: Fossils are preserved remains, impressions or traces of ancient organisms; a specimen is a sample and phylogeny is evolutionary history.

6.s: Dinosaurs were in
6.x: Dinosaurs lived in the Mesozoic era (Triassic, Jurassic, Cretaceous) and died out about 66 million years ago.

6.s: Which of the following Method is used to determine the age of the Earth ?
o: Carbon dating for the age of the fossils
6.x: The age of the Earth is found by uranium (radiometric) dating of the oldest rocks and meteorites; carbon dating works only for young organic remains.

6.s:
Find the correct statement/s:

1. Igneous rocks have no layers.

2. Limestone is white as well as black

3. Fossils are found in the igneous rocks
6.src: APPSC Assistant Motor Vehicle Inspectors, Agriculture Office
6.x: Igneous rocks have no layers and limestone occurs white as well as black (1, 2 true); fossils are not found in igneous rocks (3 false).

6.s: Which one of the following groups consists entirely of sedimentary rocks?
6.x: Sandstone, limestone, shale and conglomerate are sedimentary rocks. The other groups contain igneous or metamorphic rocks.
6.tq: Classify every option by identifying the rock type of each member.
xs: **Sandstone, limestone, shale and conglomerate** are all sedimentary — option **(1)** is correct.
Option (2) — **granite, basalt, gabbro, dolerite** — are all **igneous**.
Option (3) — **marble, slate, quartzite, gneiss** — are all **metamorphic**.
Option (4) mixes igneous (granite, basalt), sedimentary (sandstone) and metamorphic (marble).
xa: Other sedimentary rocks: **coal** and **chalk**; **coal** is sedimentary (organic).
Igneous also includes **pegmatite**; metamorphic also includes **schist**.

6.s: Sedimentary rocks are called ‘stratified rocks’ because they are generally formed as:
o: Successive layers of deposited, compacted and cemented sediments
Single layers of volcanic ash only
Metamorphosed rocks melted beneath the crust
6.x: Sediments are transported, deposited, compacted and cemented into successive layers called strata.
6.tq: Connect the descriptive term with its formation process.
xs: Sedimentary rocks form as **successive layers** of **deposited, compacted and cemented** sediments — option **(1)** is correct.
These layers are called **strata**, hence **"stratified rocks"**.
Unlayered crystallised magma (option 4) describes **igneous** rock.
xa: The hardening of sediments is called **lithification**.
Sedimentary rocks **may contain fossils** and host **coal, petroleum, natural gas**.

6.s: Which of the following pairs (mode of formation – sedimentary rock) is correctly matched?
6.x: Rock salt is chemically formed; sandstone is mechanically formed and coal organically formed.
xa: Other chemical examples: **halite, chert**.
Other organic examples: **chalk**, coral limestone, **geyserite**.
⚠ Coal is **sedimentary (organic)** — a common odd-one-out trap.

6.s: Which of the following describes clay with respect to porosity and permeability?
6.x: Clay has pore spaces, but its very fine particles prevent easy passage of water, so it is porous but impermeable.
xa: **Chalk and sandstone** are both porous and permeable.
**Granite** is neither porous nor permeable.
**Shale / clay** metamorphoses into **slate**.

6.s: Sedimentary rocks cover about what share of the Earth's surface?
6.x: Sedimentary rocks cover about 75% of the Earth's surface and hold most fossils and mineral oil.

6.s: Which rocks are the principal repositories of fossils?
6.x: Sedimentary rocks such as sandstone preserve fossils and hold coal, petroleum and natural gas.
xa: **Archaean** rocks are a **"no fossils"** zone, formed before life.
**Dravidian (Palaeozoic)** rocks are **fossil-rich**, with plenty of marine fossils.

6.s: Who developed the geological time scale in 1760?
6.x: Arduino developed it in 1760; the Standard scale was set in Italy in 1881 and the Indian scale was advocated by T.H. Holland.
xa: **J.D. Dana** coined **"Archaean"** in **1872** (some notes print 1782).
**GSI** was set up in **1851** under the **Ministry of Mines**.

6.s: What is Marble?
6.x: Marble is a metamorphic rock formed from limestone under heat and pressure.

6.s: Origin of Metamorphic rocks occurs from …….. rock ?
6.x: Metamorphic rocks form from both igneous and sedimentary rocks under heat and pressure.

6.s: Which one of the following is not associated with the 'group'?
6.x: Gneiss is metamorphic; sandstone, limestone and shale are sedimentary, so gneiss is the odd one.

6.s: Which among the following is connected with Metamorphic rock ?
6.x: Garnet is a typical metamorphic mineral; copper, manganese and pyrite are not tied to metamorphism.

6.s: Which one of the following is not an example of Metamorphic rock ?
6.x: Granite is igneous; marble, quartzite and slate are metamorphic.

6.s: Quartzite is metamorphosed from:
6.x: Quartzite is metamorphosed from quartz-rich sandstone; limestone gives marble and shale gives slate.

6.s: Quartzite is metamorphosed from :
6.x: Quartzite forms from sandstone; limestone → marble, shale → slate, obsidian is volcanic glass.

6.s: Which one of the followings is an example of Metamorphic rocks
6.src: APPSC Group-III Mains Panchayat Secretary (Grade-IV) Paper-I
6.x: Marble (from limestone) is a metamorphic rock.

6.s: Which one of the following is the odd one out?
6.x: Marble, slate and quartzite are metamorphic rocks, whereas limestone is a sedimentary rock and a parent rock of marble.
6.tq: Identify the common rock class and then locate the parent or non-metamorphic member.
xs: **Limestone** is the odd one out: it is **sedimentary** — option **(4)** is correct.
**Quartzite, marble and slate** are **metamorphic**.
Limestone is the **parent** of **marble**; shale → **slate**; sandstone → **quartzite**.
xa: ⚠ Odd-one-out trap: metamorphic rocks have non-metamorphic parents (**limestone, shale, sandstone, granite**).
**Granite → gneiss**; **coal → graphite** (via anthracite).

6.s: Which of the following is NOT a typical metamorphic mineral?
6.x: Garnet, kyanite and sillimanite are typical metamorphic minerals. Halite is associated with chemically formed sedimentary deposits.
6.tq: Find the odd mineral from a nearby sedimentary category.
xs: **Halite** is NOT a metamorphic mineral — option **(2)** is correct.
Halite is a **chemically formed sedimentary** deposit, like **rock salt** and **gypsum**.
**Garnet, kyanite, sillimanite** (and **staurolite**) are typical metamorphic minerals.
xa: Metamorphic rocks: **marble, slate, quartzite, gneiss, schist**.
Types of metamorphism: **thermal/contact** and **regional/dynamic**.

6.s: Which rock is produced by the metamorphism of limestone?
6.x: Limestone becomes marble; shale becomes slate, sandstone quartzite and coal graphite.
xa: **Granite → Gneiss** is the fourth classic pair.
Metamorphism = recrystallisation under **heat and pressure**, without melting.

6.s: What does coal finally become through metamorphism via anthracite?
6.x: Coal is metamorphosed into graphite via anthracite; slate comes from shale.

6.s: Gneiss is usually formed by the metamorphism of which rock?
6.x: Gneiss usually forms from granite; limestone gives marble, sandstone quartzite and shale slate.

6.s: Which metamorphic rock is formed from shale?
6.x: Shale (clay rock) changes into slate under heat and pressure; slate can further become schist.

6.s: Which metamorphic rock is formed from sandstone?
6.x: Sandstone recrystallises under heat and pressure into quartzite, a quartz-rich, non-foliated rock.

6.s: Into which metamorphic rocks does basalt change?
6.x: Metamorphism of basalt gives amphibolite and schist.

6.s: What are the important agents of metamorphism?
6.x: Heat and pressure transform igneous and sedimentary rocks; complete melting is not required and would lead to magma.
xa: **Melting** in the rock cycle produces **magma**, which forms **igneous** rock.
Examples: **limestone → marble**, **sandstone → quartzite**, **granite → gneiss**.

6.s: Petrology is
6.src: APPSC Group-II Paper-I General Studies & Mental Ability 2019
6.x: Petrology is the study (science) of rocks, a part of geology.

6.s:
Match the following
List-I:
(A) Shale

6.s: Carbon dioxide dissolved in rainwater helps weathering by forming which of the following?

The carbon ends up stored as **bicarbonate/limestone**.
xa: **Enhanced rock weathering**: crushed fast-weathering **basalt** on farmland locks up CO2 as **bicarbonate**.

6.s: What is the branch of geology that studies rocks called?
6.x: Petrology is the study of rocks; it recognises three types – igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic.

6.s: Enhanced rock weathering, which locks up carbon dioxide as bicarbonate, involves spreading which crushed rock on farmland?
6.x: Enhanced rock weathering spreads crushed fast-weathering basalt on farmland, where weathering locks carbon dioxide as bicarbonate.
xa: Rain CO2 forms **carbonic acid**, which weathers rock; carbon is stored as **bicarbonate/limestone**.
Glacier-crushed **pyrite** in the upper **Indus** basin releases CO2 about **three times** faster than silicate weathering removes it.

6.s: In the rock cycle, through which process do deposited sediments become sedimentary rock?
6.x: After weathering, erosion and deposition, lithification forms sedimentary rocks; heat and pressure then form metamorphic rocks and melting forms magma.
xa: Full cycle: **Magma → igneous → sedimentary → metamorphic → magma**.
**Key rule:** any rock type can turn into any other.
Sedimentary rock forms through **burial, compaction, cementation**.

6.s: In the rock cycle, what can exposed metamorphic rocks weather into?
6.x: Exposed metamorphic rocks can weather into sediment; any rock type can be transformed into another.
xa: Mantle link: rock material comes up in **eruptions**; **subducted crust** melts back into the mantle.
Cycle: **Magma → igneous → sedimentary → metamorphic → magma**.

6.s: Lithology primarily refers to the study of which of the following characteristics of a rock unit?
o: Its physical character, including texture, grain size and composition
Its magnetic field and seismic waves
6.x: Lithology describes the physical character of a rock unit, particularly its texture, grain size and composition.

xs: **Lithology** = a rock unit's **physical character** — **texture, grain size, composition** — option **(3)** is correct.
It is not limited to **age** or **fossils**.
xa: **Petrology** is the study of rocks; **uranium dating** fixes the age of very old materials.
**Geological Survey of India**: set up **1851**, under the **Ministry of Mines**.

7.s:
Which of the following are the evidence of the phenomenon of continental drift?

7.s:
Assertion (A) : Rich placer deposits of gold are found on the Ghana coast and gold-bearing veins are found in Brazil.

o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct

7.s: With which of the following was Wegener's 'pole-fleeing force' associated?
o: The gravity of the Sun and the Moon
7.x: The pole-fleeing force was linked to Earth's rotation and the tidal force to the Sun and Moon; both were too weak, so the theory was not accepted.
xa: **Arthur Holmes** (**1930s**) gave drift the driving force Wegener lacked — **convection currents**.
Wegener proposed continental drift in **1912**.

7.s: Why was Wegener's continental drift theory rejected?
o: It was based on GPS data
His proposed forces were too weak
It denied the existence of Pangaea
7.x: Wegener's pole-fleeing and tidal forces were too weak to move continents; Holmes later supplied the driving force.

7.s: In which year did Alfred Wegener put forward the theory of continental drift?
7.x: Wegener gave continental drift in 1912; Holmes (1930s), Hess (1961) and plate tectonics (1967) came later.

7.s: What was the name of the mega-ocean that surrounded Pangaea?
7.x: Panthalassa surrounded Pangaea; the Tethys Sea lay between northern Laurasia and southern Gondwanaland.
xa: Laurasia: **North America, Greenland, Europe, Asia (minus India)**.
Gondwanaland: **South America, Africa, India, Australia, Antarctica, Madagascar, Arabia**.

7.s: Which one of the following groups consists entirely of landmasses assigned to Gondwanaland?
o: South America, Africa, India, Australia and Antarctica
North America, Greenland, Europe and Asia
Europe, India, North America and Greenland
Asia, Africa, Europe and South America
7.x: Gondwanaland included South America, Africa, India, Australia, Antarctica, Madagascar and Arabia.
7.tq: Classify a group by checking every member against the southern supercontinent.
xs: **South America, Africa, India, Australia, Antarctica** were all part of **Gondwanaland** — option **(1)** is correct.
**North America, Greenland, Europe, Asia** formed **Laurasia** (options 2–4 mix in Laurasian lands).
xa: Gondwanaland also included **Madagascar** and **Arabia**.
⚠ India = **Gondwanaland**, not Laurasia (APPSC **2018**: India is part of **Gondwana Land**).

7.s: Which landmasses did the Tethys Sea separate?
7.x: Pangaea split into Laurasia in the north and Gondwanaland in the south, separated by the Tethys Sea.

7.s: Which of the following was a part of Laurasia?
7.x: Laurasia included North America, Greenland, Europe and Asia minus India; India, Australia and Madagascar were Gondwanaland.
7.tq: one-liner

7.s: Gondwana-type tillites in India and their counterparts in southern continents support continental drift. What do tillites indicate?
7.x: Tillites are glacial deposits. Their distribution across India and other southern continents indicates that these areas were formerly connected and experienced common glacial conditions.
7.tq: Identify the process represented by a geological deposit.
xs: **Tillites** are **glacial deposits**, so they indicate **ancient glacial conditions** — option **(1)** is correct.
India's **Gondwana-type tillites** have counterparts in the **other southern continents**, showing they were once joined.
xa: Other evidences: **jig-saw fit**, **same-age rocks**, **placer deposits**, **fossils** (Mesosaurus, Glossopteris).
India belonged to **Gondwanaland**, not Laurasia.

7.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Placer deposits — Ghana and Brazil source region
Same-age rocks — Brazil and Western Africa
Jigsaw fit — South America and Africa coastlines
7.x: Mesosaurus is associated with South Africa and Brazil. The other three pairs correctly represent evidence for continental drift.
7.tq: Find the incorrectly paired evidence and geographical occurrence.
xs: **Mesosaurus — India and Australia only** is wrongly matched — option **(1)** is correct.
**Mesosaurus** is found in **South Africa and Brazil**.
The other pairs are right: **placer gold** (Ghana, source in Brazil), **same-age rocks** (Brazil–Western Africa), **jig-saw fit** (South America–Africa).
xa: **Lemurs** in **India, Madagascar, Africa** gave rise to the idea of "**Lemuria**".
**Glossopteris** flora is another fossil evidence.

7.s: The ancient rock belts of about 2,000 million years on the Brazil coast match belts found in which region?
7.x: Ancient rock belts on the Brazil coast match rock belts of the same age in Western Africa.
7.tq: Connect the numerical age with the correct matching region.
xs: The **2,000-million-year** rock belts of the **Brazil coast** match those of **Western Africa** — option **(1)** is correct.
This is the "**rocks of the same age** across oceans" evidence (UPSC **2025**).
xa: **Placer gold** of the **Ghana coast** has its source in the **Brazil plateau** (UPSC **2025**).
UPSC **2025** counted rock belts, placer gold and a third evidence as **all correct**.
**Bullard's 1964** computer fit matched South America and Africa.

7.s: Who is associated with the 1964 computer fit of South America and Africa?
7.x: Bullard's 1964 computer fit supported the jig-saw fit, best at the continental-shelf edge.
7.tq: one-liner

7.s: Where are Mesosaurus fossils, an evidence of continental drift, found?
7.x: Mesosaurus occurs in South Africa and Brazil, not in India and Australia.
7.tq: one-liner

7.s: Which fossil flora is cited as an evidence of continental drift?
7.x: Glossopteris fossils occur in India and the other southern continents, showing they were once joined in Gondwanaland.

7.s: About how many years ago did Gondwanaland break up?
7.x: Gondwanaland broke up approximately 225 million years ago.
7.tq: Distinguish the geological breakup date from the later Himalayan uplift date.
xs: **Gondwanaland broke up ~225 million years ago** — option **(3)** is correct.
**65 million years ago** is when the **Himalayas rose**, not the break-up.
xa: After the break-up, the **Indian craton** slid towards the **Eurasian craton**.
India moves **north at ~5 cm/year** into the Eurasian plate.

7.s: The theory that states "pieces of the Earth's crust are in constant, slow motion driven by movement in the mantle" is called:

7.s: Based on following statements choose the correct option: Statement - I : Theory of Plate tectonics was given by H.H. Hess in 1967. Statement - II : Theory of Plate Tectonics is based on Theory of Seafloor Spreading.
o: Statement - I and Statement - II both are true
Statement - I and Statement- II both are false
Statement - I is true but Statement - II is false
Statement - I is false but Statement - II is true

7.s: Based on following statements choose the correct option: Statement - I : Theory of Plate tectonics was given by H.H. Hess in 1967 Statement - II : Theory of Plate Tectonics is based on Theory of Sea floor Spreading
o: Statement - I and Statement - II both are true
Statement - I and Statement- II both are false
Statement - I is true but Statement - II is false
Statement - I is false but Statement - II is true
7.x: Statement I is false (plate tectonics: McKenzie, Parker, Morgan 1967; Hess gave sea-floor spreading); Statement II is true.

7.s: How many plates does the 'theory of Plate Tectonics' consist of?
7.src: APPSC Degree Lecturers General Studies & Mental Ability 2020
7.x: Plate tectonics recognises seven major plates (Pacific, N. American, S. American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian, Antarctic).

7.s: Which one of the following is a major plate?
7.x: The Pacific Plate is one of the seven major plates; Cocos, Arabian and Philippine are minor plates.

7.s: Cocos Plate lies between-
7.x: The Cocos Plate lies between Central America and the Pacific Plate; Nazca lies off South America.

7.s: Who proposed the convection current theory as an explanation for the movement of crustal plates?
7.x: Arthur Holmes proposed the convection current theory in the 1930s.
7.tq: Distinguish the proponent of the driving mechanism from proponents of continental drift and sea-floor spreading.
xs: **Arthur Holmes** proposed the **convection current theory** (**1930s**) — option **(4)** is correct.
**Wegener** gave continental drift (**1912**); **Harry Hess** sea-floor spreading (**1961**); **Vine** (with Matthews) explained magnetic stripes (**1963**).
xa: **Radioactive decay heat** in the mantle drives the convection currents.
Plate tectonics' driving force is **mantle convection** (Arthur Holmes).

7.s: In Holmes's convection-current theory, what is the source of the heat that drives mantle convection?
7.x: Radioactive heat drives convection; rising limbs split crust at ridges and sinking limbs drag plates at trenches.
xa: Holmes gave drift the **driving force Wegener lacked**.
**Hess (1961)**: magma rises at **mid-oceanic ridges**; crust is destroyed at **trenches**.

7.s: The theory of plate tectonics was put together in 1967 by McKenzie and Parker and independently by whom?
7.x: McKenzie and Parker developed the theory in 1967, and Morgan proposed it independently.
7.tq: Pair the principal proponents with the correct year and contribution.
xs: Plate tectonics was put together in **1967** by **McKenzie and Parker**, and independently by **Morgan** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Wegener** = drift (**1912**); **Holmes** = convection (**1930s**); **Bullard** = jig-saw computer fit (**1964**).
xa: The lithosphere is broken into **rigid plates** floating on the semi-fluid **asthenosphere**.
Driving force: **mantle convection**.

7.s: On which layer do the lithospheric plates float?
7.x: The rigid lithosphere is broken into plates that float on the semi-fluid asthenosphere.
7.tq: Distinguish the rigid layer from the underlying semi-fluid layer.
xs: Lithospheric plates float on the **semi-fluid asthenosphere** — option **(2)** is correct.
The lithosphere is broken into **rigid plates**.
xa: Plate tectonics: **1967**, **McKenzie and Parker**, independently **Morgan**.
There are **seven major plates** (APPSC **2018**).

7.s: Which one of the following is NOT one of the seven major plates listed in plate tectonics?
7.x: The seven listed major plates are Pacific, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian and Antarctic. Nazca is a minor plate.
7.tq: Separate a minor plate from the standard list of major plates.
xs: The **Nazca** plate is a **minor** plate, not one of the seven major — option **(1)** is correct.
The **7 major plates**: **Pacific, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian, Antarctic**.
xa: Minor plates: **Cocos, Nazca, Arabian, Philippine, Caroline, Fuji**.
Nazca lies between **South America** and the **Pacific plate**.

7.s: Between which plates does the Nazca Plate lie?
7.x: The Nazca Plate is located between the South American Plate and the Pacific Plate.
7.tq: Test a minor plate by its bordering major plates.
xs: The **Nazca** plate lies between **South America** and the **Pacific plate** — option **(3)** is correct.
**Caroline** = between the Philippine and Indian plates; **Philippine** = between the Asiatic and Pacific plates; **Owen Fracture** separates African and Indian plates.
xa: ⚠ **Cocos** = Central America; **Nazca** = South America.
In the **Andes**, the **Nazca** plate subducts under the **South American** plate.

7.s: Which instrument-based method is used to monitor plate movement?
7.x: Plate movement is monitored using GPS data.
7.tq: Distinguish the modern monitoring technology from unrelated instruments.
xs: Plate movement is monitored using **GPS data** — option **(3)** is correct (APPSC **2021**).
Tide gauges, barometers and rain gauges measure sea level, pressure and rain — not plate motion.
xa: **GSI** runs **34 GNSS stations** tracking crustal movement and building strain models.
India moves **north at ~5 cm/year** into the Eurasian plate.

7.s: Between which plates does the Caroline Plate lie?
7.x: The Caroline Plate lies between the Philippine and Indian plates, north of New Guinea.
7.tq: one-liner

7.s: How many major lithospheric plates are there?
7.x: There are seven major plates: Pacific, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian and Antarctic.

7.s: Between which plates does the Philippine Plate lie?
7.x: The Philippine Plate is a minor plate lying between the Asiatic and Pacific plates.

7.s: Which landmass mostly forms the Arabian Plate?
7.x: The Arabian Plate is a minor plate made up mostly of the Saudi Arabian landmass.

7.s: What is the cause of earthquakes in the region from the Himalayas to the Arakan Yoma?
o: Collision of Pacific Plate and Indian Plate
Collision of Indian Plate and Tibetan Plate
Collision of Eurasian Plate and Indian Plate
Construction of dams on the Ganga and Brahma putra
7.x: Earthquakes from the Himalayas to the Arakan Yoma come from the collision of the Indian Plate with the Eurasian Plate.

7.s: The North-Western Region of the Indian Sub-continent is susceptible to earthquake activity because of –
7.x: The north-west of the subcontinent lies on the convergent Indian–Eurasian plate boundary, so earthquakes come from plate tectonic activity, not volcanoes or corals.

7.s:
Given below are two statements, one is labelled as-
Assertion (A) and the other as
Reason (R).
Assertion (A): The Himalayas are still rising.
Reason (R) : The Indian tectonic plate is colliding with the Eurasian plate.
Select the correct answer from the codes given below:
o: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct
7.x: Both true and R explains A: the Indian plate still pushes into the Eurasian plate (~5 cm/yr), so the Himalayas keep rising.

7.s: The paleomagnetic results obtained from India indicate that in the past, the Indian land mass has moved :
7.x: Palaeomagnetic results show the Indian landmass has moved northward from south of the equator.

7.s: Which of the following mainly explains the Himalayas and the Indo-Gangetic foreland basin?
o: Collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates
7.x: The India-Eurasia collision explains the Himalayas, the Indo-Gangetic foreland basin and India's earthquake risk.
xa: The collision began **~4–5 crore (40–50 million) years ago**.
The Indian plate **closed the Tethys**; the Himalayas are **still rising**.

7.s: What does delamination in southern Tibet refer to in the context of the Indian Plate?
o: The melting of all continental crust at the surface of Tibet
The spreading apart of the Tibetan Plateau along a mid-ocean ridge
The peeling off and sinking of the denser lower layer of the plate into the mantle at about 100 km depth
The horizontal sliding of the entire Indian Plate along the Himalayan Frontal Fault
7.x: Delamination refers to the denser lower layer of the plate peeling away and sinking into the mantle at approximately 100 kilometres depth.
7.tq: Test the exact meaning of a specialised tectonic term through its mechanism and depth.
xs: **Delamination** = the denser lower layer **peeling off and sinking into the mantle** at ~**100 km** — option **(3)** is correct.
It was seen with **94 seismic stations** in southern Tibet (seismic imaging, **helium isotopes**).
xa: India **underthrust** Asia **45–20 million years ago**, lifting the Tibetan Plateau.
The **Ladakh Magmatic Arc** lies between the **Indus and Shyok** suture zones.

7.s: What was the Indian Plate doing when the Deccan Traps erupted?
o: crossing near the equator and passing over the Reunion hotspot
moving southward across the Tethys Sea
colliding with the Eurasian Plate in the Himalaya
7.x: The Deccan Traps erupted as the northward-moving Indian Plate crossed near the equator and passed over the Reunion hotspot.
7.tq: Connect a geological event with the plate’s position and hotspot passage at that time.
xs: The **Deccan Traps** erupted as India crossed **near the equator** over the **Reunion hotspot** — option **(2)** is correct.
India was moving **northward**, not southward; collision with Eurasia came later.
xa: ⚠ **Reunion hotspot** = Deccan Traps; **Owen Fracture** = African/Indian plates.
India was **far south** of the equator before the **Cretaceous**.

7.s: About when did the collision between the Indian and Eurasian plates begin?
7.x: The collision began approximately 4–5 crore years ago, equivalent to about 40–50 million years ago. Some older estimates place it at about 50–55 million years ago.
7.tq: Convert crore-based geological time into its equivalent million-year scale without changing the order of magnitude.
xs: The India–Eurasia collision began **~4–5 crore (40–50 million) years ago** — option **(1)** is correct.
⚠ Older notes say **50–55 million** years.
xa: The Indian plate **subducted** under Eurasia and **closed the Tethys**.
India **underthrust** Asia **45–20 million years ago**, lifting the **Tibetan Plateau**.

7.s: At what rate is the Indian Plate moving northward?
7.x: The Indian Plate moves north at about 5 cm a year, so the young fold Himalayas are still rising.
xa: Uplift phases: **Eocene, Miocene and Pliocene**; began **~70 million years ago**.
The **Siwaliks** are the **youngest** range.

7.s: Until which period was the Peninsular Plateau of India a part of the African landmass?
7.x: The Peninsular Plateau, an old Gondwana shield, was part of the African landmass until the Cretaceous.
xa: **Gondwanaland broke up ~225 million years ago**.
AP's **Eastern Ghats** are old, eroded hills of the stable **Gondwana shield**, not young fold mountains.

7.s: At about what rate are the Himalayas still rising?
7.x: India moves north at about 5 cm a year, so the Himalayas are still rising by about 5 mm a year.

7.s:
Consider the following statements:

A. The Earth's magnetic field has reversed every few hundred thousand years.

B. When the Earth was created more than 4000 million years ago, there was 54% Oxygen and no Carbon dioxide.

C. When living organisms originated, they modified the early atmosphere of the Earth.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
7.x: The magnetic field has reversed many times (A true); the early atmosphere had no free oxygen, not 54% (B false); life (photosynthesis) changed the atmosphere (C true) → A and C only.

7.s: The age, density, and thickness of oceanic crust ____ with distance from the mid-ocean ridge.
7.src: APPSC Assistant Director of Economics, Assistant Commissione
7.x: Away from the mid-ocean ridge the age, density and thickness of oceanic crust (and sediment) increase.

7.s: The process that continually adds new crust is:
7.x: Sea-floor spreading at mid-ocean ridges continually adds new crust; subduction destroys it.

7.s: Who proposed the sea-floor spreading hypothesis in the early 1960s?
7.x: Harry Hess proposed the sea-floor spreading hypothesis in the early 1960s, including the creation of new crust at mid-ocean ridges and its destruction at trenches.
7.tq: Use direct person–theory identification and distinguish the proponent from related plate-tectonic thinkers.
xs: **Harry Hess** proposed **sea-floor spreading** in **1961** (early 1960s) — option **(4)** is correct.
**Wegener** = continental drift (**1912**); **Arthur Holmes** = convection currents (**1930s**).
xa: Magma rises at **mid-oceanic ridges**, new crust spreads sideways and is destroyed at **trenches**.
**Vine and Matthews (1963)** explained the **symmetrical magnetic bands** supporting it.

7.s: How do normal and reversed magnetic polarity bands occur on either side of a mid-ocean ridge?
7.x: Ridge rocks preserve the field of their time, giving alternating normal and reversed bands symmetrically on both sides.
xa: The bands were explained by **Vine and Matthews, 1963**.
**Brunhes–Matuyama** reversal: **780,000** years ago.

7.s: Who explained in 1963 the symmetrical normal and reversed magnetic bands on either side of a ridge?
7.x: Vine and Matthews (1963) explained the palaeomagnetic stripes; McKenzie and Parker put plate tectonics together in 1967.

7.s: The direct observation of sea-floor spreading in bursts was associated with which conclusion?
o: Sea-floor spreading occurs only at continental interiors.
Sea-floor spreading may take place in episodic bursts.
Sea-floor spreading always occurs at a constant rate.
Sea-floor spreading is unrelated to lava outpouring.
7.x: The observed rapid episode of sinking, spreading and lava emplacement suggested that sea-floor spreading can occur in bursts rather than at a uniform rate.
7.tq: Infer the process characteristic from the observed event rather than from a general definition.
xs: The first direct in-situ observation showed **sea-floor spreading happens in bursts** — option **(2)** is correct.
The seafloor sank **4 m**, spread over **1 m**, with **160 million cubic metres** of lava in **16 days**.
xa: **Harry Hess (1961)**: magma rises at **mid-oceanic ridges** and new crust spreads sideways.
Crust age, density and thickness **increase with distance from the ridge** (APPSC **2019**).

7.s: Moving away from a mid-ocean ridge, which one of the following trends is observed in oceanic crust and its sediment cover?
o: Age increases, while density and thickness decrease.
Only sediment thickness increases; crustal age and density remain unchanged.
Age, density and thickness decrease continuously.
7.x: The age, density and thickness of oceanic crust, along with the thickness of its sediment cover, increase with distance from the ridge.
7.tq: Apply the directional trend rule by comparing conditions near the ridge with those farther away.
xs: Away from the ridge, **age, density and thickness increase** — option **(1)** is correct (APPSC **2019**).
The **sediment cover** also thickens with distance from the ridge.
xa: Ocean-floor rocks are **far younger** than continental rocks; the oldest are ~**200 million years**.
New crust forms at the **ridge** and is destroyed at **trenches**.

7.s: The oldest rocks of the ocean floor are approximately how old?
7.x: Ocean-floor rocks are much younger than continental rocks; the oldest are about 200 million years old.

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
8.x: The Narmada flows west because it occupies a linear rift valley; lying between the Vindhyas and Satpuras only describes where the rift is, and the land of Central India does not generally slope west (UPSC key: 1 only).

8.s: 'Horsts' are features associated with
8.x: Horsts are uplifted fault blocks, i.e. block mountains (e.g. Vosges, Black Forest); grabens are the down-faulted blocks between them.

8.s: What is an elongated depression formed when the central block subsides between faults as the crust pulls apart called?
8.x: A rift valley forms when the central block sinks between faults after divergence, producing a long depression.
n: A rift valley is an elongated depression associated with faulting. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Rift valleys form through divergence or tension. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Divergence or tension causes faulting in rift-valley formation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Faulting causes the central block to subside in rift-valley formation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Tectonic faulting forms rift valleys. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
A hanging valley is glacial, whereas a rift valley is tectonic. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xa: A **graben** is a **down-faulted block** (rift valley); a **horst** an **uplifted** one.
Examples: **Death Valley** (USA), **Rhine Rift Valley**, **Narmada** and **Tapi** valleys.
⚠ A **rift valley** is **tectonic**; a **hanging valley** is **glacial**.

8.s: Which one of the following correctly matches the landform with its geographical association?
o: Vosges and Black Forest — horsts flanking the Rhine graben
Great Rift Valley — horst containing Lake Malawi
Death Valley — fold mountain of the Alps
Rhine Valley — volcanic depression of Japan
8.x: The Vosges in France and the Black Forest in Germany are horsts flanking the Rhine rift valley, which is a graben. The Great Rift Valley and Death Valley are grabens.
8.tq: Start from the sure location pair and distinguish horst margins from graben depressions.
xs: **Vosges (France)** and **Black Forest (Germany)** are **horsts** flanking the **Rhine rift valley** (graben) — option **(1)** is correct.
The **Great Rift Valley** is a **graben** (not a horst) holding **Lake Malawi**.
**Death Valley** (California) is a **graben**, not an Alpine fold.
xa: Uplifted block = **horst**; lowered block = **graben** (rift valley).
Horsts = block mountains (APPSC **2022**).

8.s: Which of the following is NOT a graben?
o: Great Rift Valley of East Africa
8.x: Sierra Nevada is a block mountain (horst), not a graben; the Great Rift Valley, Death Valley and Rhine Rift Valley are grabens.
xa: ⚠ UPSC **2024**: "Vosges – Central Asia – fold" and "Alps – block" were the **wrong** pairs.
Block mountains form when large areas **break and are displaced vertically**.

8.s: Between which ranges does the westward-flowing Narmada river lie in a rift valley?
o: The Satpuras to the north and the Vindhyas to the south
The Vindhyas to the north and the Satpuras to the south
The Aravallis to the north and the Vindhyas to the south
The Satpuras to the north and the Ajanta range to the south
8.x: The Narmada flows west through a rift valley situated between the Vindhyas in the north and the Satpuras in the south.
xa: A rift valley is a **graben** — a lowered block.
Other grabens: **Great Rift Valley**, **Death Valley**, **Rhine** valley.

8.s: What is an uplifted fault block associated with block mountains called?
8.x: Horsts are uplifted fault blocks, while grabens are down-faulted blocks; together they are associated with block mountains.
n: Horsts and grabens are associated with block mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xa: **Vosges** (France) and **Black Forest** (Germany) are horsts flanking the **Rhine rift valley**.
**Death Valley** (USA) is a graben; **Lake Malawi** lies in the **Great Rift Valley**.
**Narmada** and **Tapi** flow west through **rift valleys**.

8.s: In a normal fault, what are the force and the movement of the hanging wall?
8.x: A normal fault forms under tension with the hanging wall moving down; a reverse fault forms under compression with it moving up.

8.s: A strike-slip fault results from which force?
8.x: Strike-slip faults form by shear and involve horizontal movement.

8.s: Between which mountains does the Rhine graben lie?
8.x: The Rhine graben lies between the Vosges and the Black Forest block mountains.

8.s:
Consider the following statements about the Narmada river:
1. It flows westward through a rift valley between the Vindhyas and the Satpuras.
2. It forms a large delta at its mouth.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
8.x: The Narmada flows west in a rift valley and forms an estuary, not a delta.

8.s: Which of the following ranges is the most recent one?
8.x: The Himalayas (Tertiary) are the youngest of these; the Aravallis are the oldest, and the Vindhyas and Eastern Ghats are ancient Peninsular features.

8.s: Which among the following is most recently formed mountain range?
8.x: The Shiwaliks (outer Himalaya, formed last – Mio-Pliocene) are the most recently formed range; Vindhya, Aravalli and Annamalai are far older.

8.s:
When you travel in Himalayas, you will see the following:
1. Deep gorges
2. U-turn river courses
3. Parallel mountain ranges
4. Steep gradients causing land sliding
Which of the above can be said to be the evidence for the Himalayas being young fold mountains?
8.x: All four – deep gorges, U-turn river courses, parallel ranges and steep, landslide-prone slopes – show the Himalaya is young and still rising (UPSC key d).

8.s:
When you travel in Himalayas, you will see the following
1. Deep gorges
2. U-turn river courses
3. Parallel mountain ranges
4. Steep gradients causing landsliding
Which of the above can be said to be the evidences for Himalayas being young fold mountains ?
8.x: Deep gorges, U-turn courses, parallel ranges and landslide-prone steep gradients are all evidence of the Himalaya being young fold mountains.

8.s: As a result of which of the following were the Himalaya formed through the uplift of Tethys sediments?
o: The vertical subsidence of the Eurasian Plate during the Palaeozoic
The southward movement of the Indian Plate during the Precambrian
The volcanic eruption of the Deccan Plateau during the Quaternary
The northward movement of the Indian Plate from the Eocene to the Pliocene
8.x: The Himalaya formed when Tethys sediments were pushed upward by the northward-moving Indian Plate. Uplift began about 70 million years ago and continues even today.
8.tq: Link the mountain range with its plate movement, sedimentary source and geological time span.
xs: Tethys sediments were pushed up by the **northward-moving Indian plate** from the **Eocene to the Pliocene** — option **(4)** is correct.
The movement was northward, not southward; Precambrian and Palaeozoic are wrong ages.
xa: Uplift began ~**70 million years ago** and **continues**.
It was the **Tethys geosyncline** uplift of the **Tertiary / Aryan era**.

8.s: Earthquakes are
8.src: Inspector of Factories, Civil Assistant Surgeons & Fisheries
8.x: Earthquakes, volcanism and diastrophism come from forces inside the Earth, so they are endogenic processes; weathering and erosion are exogenic.

8.s: Identify the incorrect _ statement:
o: Geomorphic processes bring about changes in the configuration of the surface of the Earth
The endogenic and exogenic forces cause physical stresses and chemical actions on earth materials
Orogeny is the continental building process
8.x: Orogeny is the mountain-building process; epeirogeny is the continent-building process (uplift or warping of large areas), so statement (d) is the incorrect one. The other three statements are from NCERT as written.

8.s: Folding is the result of-
8.x: Folding results from orogenic (horizontal, compressional) forces; epeirogenic forces are vertical, Coriolis force deflects winds, exogenic forces act on the surface.

8.s: Which of the following processes do not come under diastrophism?
8.x: Diastrophism covers orogeny, epeirogeny, earthquakes and plate tectonics; 'heterogenic' is not a diastrophic process.

8.s: Epeirogenic forces are result of :
8.x: Epeirogenic (continent-building) forces act vertically (radially), causing uplift or subsidence of large areas; orogenic forces are horizontal.

8.s: What do mantle dynamics, produced by endogenic processes, in turn produce?
8.x: Endogenic processes produce mantle dynamics, and mantle dynamics produce plate movement; weathering and erosion are exogenic.
n: Endogenic processes drive mantle dynamics. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Mantle dynamics drive plate movement. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Mantle movement drives plate movement. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]

8.s: What are mountain-building movements caused mainly by horizontal (tangential) forces called?
8.x: Orogenic movements build mountains through horizontal forces in narrow belts; epeirogenic movements are vertical uplift or subsidence of large areas.
xa: "Vertical (radial)" forces = epeirogenic was asked in UKPSC **2024**.
The **Peninsular block** escaped folding but had **vertical movements** → epeirogenic effect.

8.s: The vertical movements of the Peninsular Block, including transgression and regression, are examples of which type of diastrophic effect?
8.x: The Peninsular Block largely escaped folding but experienced vertical movements such as transgression and regression, representing an epeirogenic effect.
8.tq: Apply the horizontal-versus-vertical movement distinction to a regional example.
xs: The Peninsular block's **vertical movements** (**transgression, regression**) are an **epeirogenic effect** — option **(3)** is correct.
It **escaped folding**, so it is not an **orogenic** effect.
xa: Epeirogeny = **continent building**: uplift or warping of large continental areas by **vertical (radial)** forces.
Orogeny = **mountain building** by severe folding in long narrow belts.

8.s: What are the processes that move, raise or build up the Earth's crust, including earthquakes and plate movements, collectively called?
8.x: Diastrophism covers all crustal movements that move, raise or build up the crust, including earthquakes and plate movements, not just folding.
xa: ⚠ "**Heterogenic**" is NOT included (MPPSC **2023**).
Orogenic = **horizontal** forces; epeirogenic = **vertical** forces.

8.s: Weathering and erosion are examples of which processes?
8.x: Weathering and erosion are exogenic processes, not part of diastrophism.

8.s: An upfold in rock is
8.x: An anticline is an upfold (upward-convex arch); a syncline is a downfold, and a graben or horse is a fault feature.

8.s: The type of folds where both limbs of the fold becomes horizontal and parallel is known as
8.x: In a recumbent fold the axial plane is essentially horizontal, so both limbs lie horizontal and parallel; an overturned fold is still inclined.

8.s: What is a recumbent fold that is broken and thrust far forward called?
8.x: A nappe is a strongly displaced recumbent fold that has been broken and thrust far forward.
xa: **Anticline** = up-arch; **syncline** = down-trough.
The **Siwaliks** are simple anticline-syncline folds, **Jura type**.

8.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
8.x: Cuddapah sediments were laid down in synclinal troughs; the Siwaliks show simple Jura-type anticline–syncline folds, not block structures.

8.s: What is a fold whose two limbs are parallel called?
8.x: An isoclinal fold has parallel limbs.

8.s: Which fold form develops immediately before a nappe?
8.x: With rising pressure a recumbent fold breaks along a thrust and is pushed forward to form a nappe.

8.s: What is mountain building by folding and faulting due to horizontal (tangential) forces called?
8.x: Orogenic movements act through horizontal forces and build mountains such as the Himalayas.

8.s: Which forces mainly cause epeirogenic movements?
8.x: Epeirogenic movements are vertical and uplift or warp continents and plateaus.

8.s:
Consider the following statements about diastrophism:
1. Orogenic movements uplift or warp whole continents and plateaus.
2. Sudden movements such as earthquakes and volcanoes are treated separately.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
8.x: Uplift or warping of continents is epeirogenic, not orogenic; sudden movements are treated separately.

8.s:
Consider the following statements about the development of folds with increasing pressure:
1. A symmetrical fold comes before an asymmetrical fold.
2. A nappe forms before a recumbent fold.
3. A recumbent fold forms after an asymmetrical fold.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
8.x: The order is symmetrical, asymmetrical, recumbent and finally nappe, so a nappe forms after (not before) a recumbent fold.

8.s: In plate-tectonic terms, what are the Eastern Ghats?
o: Old, highly eroded, discontinuous hills of the stable Gondwana shield
Block mountains of recently uplifted nappes
Young fold mountains formed by recent continental collision
Volcanic hills formed along a rift
8.x: The Eastern Ghats are old, highly eroded and discontinuous hills of the stable Gondwana shield, not young fold mountains.
xa: The Peninsular plateau is an old **Gondwana shield**, part of the African landmass until the **Cretaceous**.
Old fold example in India: the **Aravallis**.

8.s: What are an up-arched fold and a down-troughed fold respectively called?
8.x: An anticline is an up-arched fold, while a syncline is a down-troughed fold. Horst and graben are fault blocks, not folds.
8.tq: Discriminate between the commonly confused anticline-syncline pair by their shapes.
xs: An up-arch is an **anticline** and a down-trough a **syncline** — option **(2)** is correct.
**Horst and graben** are **fault blocks** (block mountains), not folds.
**Nappe** and **overfold** are stages of folding under rising pressure.
xa: Folds are caused by **compression**.
Sequence: symmetrical → asymmetrical → **overfold** → recumbent → **nappe**.
The **Siwaliks** have simple anticline-syncline folds of the **"Jura" type**.

8.s: Which one of the following is an old fold mountain range?
8.x: The Aravallis are old, worn-down fold mountains and are among the oldest mountain systems in India.
8.tq: Use an odd-age association to distinguish an old fold range from the listed young fold ranges.
xs: The **Aravallis** are **old, worn-down** fold mountains — among India's oldest — option **(2)** is correct.
**Himalayas, Alps, Andes** are **young fold** mountains (Tertiary / **Alpine orogeny**).
xa: Other old folds: **Appalachians** (North America), **Urals** (Europe–Asia divide).
The **Rockies** (North America) are young fold mountains.
AP's **Eastern Ghats** are old, eroded hills of the **Gondwana shield**, not young folds.

8.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Alps – Young fold mountains of Europe
Appalachians – Old fold mountains of North America
Urals – Old fold mountains along the Europe–Asia divide
Rockies – Old fold mountains of North America
8.x: The Rockies are young fold mountains of North America; the Appalachians are the old ones.
xa: The **Himalayas** (Asia) and **Andes** (South America) are also young.
The **Aravallis** are one of India's oldest fold ranges.

8.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Himalayas?
o: Their formation began about 70 million years ago and continues at present
They were formed from sediments of the Tethys Sea
Their uplift is associated with the Eocene, Miocene and Pliocene epochs
The Siwaliks are the oldest Himalayan range
8.x: The Siwaliks are the youngest Himalayan range, not the oldest.
xa: India moves **north at ~5 cm/year** into the Eurasian plate.
The Himalayas are a **continent–continent** convergent boundary (**Indian vs Eurasian**).

8.s: With rising pressure, which fold forms next after an asymmetrical fold?
8.x: The sequence is symmetrical, asymmetrical, overfold, recumbent and nappe.

8.s: Which one of the following is NOT an old fold mountain?
8.x: The Rockies are young (Tertiary/Alpine) fold mountains; the Aravallis, Appalachians and Urals are old, worn-down folds.

8.s: Which is the youngest Himalayan range, with simple Jura-type folds?
8.x: The Siwaliks are the youngest Himalayan range and show simple Jura-type folds.

8.s: The Indo-Gangetic Plain is bounded by which of the following fault systems?
o: Two thrust faults on both sides
A normal fault in the north and the Himalayan Frontal Fault in the south
The Himalayan Frontal Fault in the north and a normal fault in the south
Two strike-slip faults in the north and south
8.x: The Indo-Gangetic Plain is bounded by the Himalayan Frontal Fault to the north and a normal fault to the south.
8.tq: Test the location and type of the bounding structures together.
xs: The **Indo-Gangetic plain** is bounded by the **Himalayan Frontal Fault** (north) and a **normal fault** (south) — option **(3)** is correct.
Option (2) reverses the two.
xa: The **HFF** is one of the Himalayan **thrusts**, with **MCT** and **MBT**.
Plate collision explains the **Indo-Gangetic foreland basin**.

8.s: Which of the following is an example of a block mountain in India?
8.x: The Satpura is a block mountain, flanked by the rift valleys of the Narmada and Tapi.
xa: Uplifted blocks = **horsts**; sunken blocks = **grabens**.
The **Red Sea** is also a rift.

8.s: The Himalayan MCT, MBT and HFF are examples of which one of the following?
8.x: The Himalayan Main Central Thrust, Main Boundary Thrust and Himalayan Frontal Fault are examples of thrust faults.
8.tq: Test the association between named regional structures and the correct fault type.
xs: The Himalayan **MCT, MBT and HFF** are **thrust faults** — option **(3)** is correct.
A thrust is a **low-angle reverse fault** caused by **compression**.
**San Andreas** and **Sagaing** are **strike-slip**; **Rio Grande** and **East African Rift** are **normal** faults.
xa: The **Indo-Gangetic plain** is bounded by the **Himalayan Frontal Fault** (north) and a **normal fault** (south).
A **nappe** is a recumbent fold broken by a **thrust**.

8.s: What is a low-angle reverse fault called?
8.x: A thrust fault is a low-angle reverse fault; in a normal fault the hanging wall moves down and a strike-slip fault moves horizontally.

8.s: Which lake lies at the southern end of the East African Rift?
8.x: The East African Rift holds a series of mostly freshwater lakes with Lake Malawi at its southern end; Lake Victoria lies between the two branches and is not a rift lake.
xa: ⚠ APPSC G1 **2024** keyed statements **I, II, III** on this rift.
The **Red Sea** is also a rift; with the East African Rift it meets at the **Afar triple junction**.

8.s: In the Vosges–Rhine example, what is the Rhine Valley?
8.x: The Rhine Valley is a graben (sunken block); the Vosges are horsts, i.e. block mountains.

8.s: The Satpura is a block mountain lying between the rift valleys of which rivers?
8.x: The Satpura is a block mountain between the rift valleys of the Narmada and Tapi.

8.s: What are horsts also known as?
8.x: A horst is an uplifted block between faults, so it forms a block mountain; a sunken block (graben) forms a rift valley.

8.s: Which of the following lakes is NOT a rift lake of the East African Rift?
8.x: Lake Victoria lies in a shallow basin between the rift arms, so it is not a rift lake; Lake Malawi lies at the rift's southern end.

8.s: Which force produces a normal fault?
8.x: A normal fault forms under tension, with the hanging wall moving down; reverse and thrust faults form under compression.

8.s: In a reverse fault, which force acts and how does the hanging wall move?
8.x: A reverse fault forms under compression and its hanging wall moves up; a normal fault forms under tension.

8.s: What is isostasy?
o: Continuous erosion of mountains by running water
Horizontal movement of plates across ocean floors
Formation of folds exclusively by compression
Balance of crustal blocks floating on denser material below
8.x: Isostasy refers to the gravitational balance of crustal blocks floating on denser underlying material.
8.tq: Select the definition that expresses crustal buoyancy and balance.
xs: **Isostasy** is the **balance of crustal blocks "floating"** on denser material below — option **(4)** is correct.
Plate movement, erosion and compression folding are different processes.
xa: **Airy**: crust of **uniform density**, different thickness; mountains have deep **"roots"**.
**Pratt**: crust of **different density**, uniform **depth of compensation**; higher blocks are **lighter**.

8.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Airy and Pratt concepts of isostasy?
o: Airy assumes uniform crustal density but varying crustal thickness.
In Pratt's concept, higher blocks are denser.
Pratt assumes varying crustal densities with a uniform depth of compensation.
In Airy's concept, mountains possess deep roots.
8.x: In Pratt's concept higher blocks are lighter, not denser. The other three statements correctly describe Airy (uniform density, varying thickness, deep roots) and Pratt (varying density, common compensation depth).
xa: ⚠ Airy = same density, different thickness; Pratt = different density, same depth.
Isostasy = balance of crustal blocks **floating** on denser material.

8.s: Who proposed the geosynclinal theory associated with long, shallow sediment-filled troughs between rigid forelands?
8.x: Kober proposed the geosynclinal theory. It describes long, shallow sinking sea troughs between rigid forelands or kratogens, where sediments accumulate before being compressed into mountains.
8.tq: Identify the theorist from the central concept and its terminology.
xs: **Kober** proposed the **geosynclinal theory** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Geosynclines** (long, shallow, sinking sea troughs) collect sediments between rigid forelands (**kratogens**), which squeeze them into mountains.
**Airy** and **Pratt** gave isostasy models; **Wegener** gave continental drift.
xa: Stages: **lithogenesis → orogenesis → gliptogenesis**.
Indian example: the **Tethys geosyncline** uplifted into the **Himalaya**.

8.s: In Kober's geosynclinal theory, which is the first stage, marked by sedimentation?
8.x: Kober's stages are lithogenesis (sedimentation), orogenesis (folding and mountain building) and gliptogenesis (uplift and denudation).

8.s: In Kober's geosynclinal theory, what are the rigid forelands bordering a geosyncline called?
8.x: Kober's geosynclines are long shallow troughs between rigid kratogens that are squeezed into mountains.

8.s: What does Pratt's concept of isostasy assume?
o: Varying density with the same compensation depth
8.x: Pratt assumed varying density and the same compensation depth, so higher blocks are lighter; Airy assumed uniform density and deep roots.

9.s: The tallest mountain measured from top to bottom is ____ which stands tall for more than 10000 meters
9.src: APPSC Forest Section Officer General Studies & Mental Abilit
9.at: Mauna Kea, an inactive volcano on island of Hawaii

9.s: Which of the following is the World's largest volcano erupted for the first time in 38 years?
o: More than one of the above
9.x: Mauna Loa (Hawaii), the world's largest active volcano by volume, erupted on 27 Nov 2022 – its first eruption since 1984 (38 years).

9.s: Which Volcano is called 'the lighthouse' of Mediterranean Sea ?
9.x: Stromboli (Aeolian/Lipari Islands, Italy) erupts every few minutes and has been active for centuries, so it is called the 'Lighthouse of the Mediterranean'.

9.s: In which country did the White Island Volcano erupt in December 2019?
9.src: APPSC Junior Lecturers General Studies & Mental Ability 2020
9.x: Whakaari / White Island, New Zealand erupted on 9 December 2019, killing 22 people.

9.s: Where is the volcanic mountain, Mount St. Helens, located? Geography Mapping PMF IAS Geo – 142
9.x: Mount St. Helens is an active stratovolcano in Washington State, USA (great eruption of 18 May 1980).

9.s: Mauna Loa is an active volcano in –
9.x: Mauna Loa is an active shield volcano on the Island of Hawaii (USA).

9.s: Cotpaxi is situated in
9.x: Cotopaxi is an active stratovolcano in the Andes of Ecuador; South America is the continent, not the country asked for.

9.s:
Which of the following are active volcanoes ?
1. Aconcagua
2. Cotopaxi
3. Etna
4. Fujiyama
Select the correct answer from the code given below :
9.x: Cotopaxi, Etna and Fujiyama count as active volcanoes (Fuji last erupted 1707 but is classed active); Aconcagua is not an active volcano.

9.s: Where is the mount Saint Helens situated ?
9.x: Mount St. Helens is in Washington State, USA.

9.s: Tungurahua Volcano, which was declared a Global Geopark by UNESCO in 2025, is situated in which one among the following countries?
9.x: Tungurahua ('throat of fire') is an active Andean volcano near Baños, Ecuador; UNESCO designated the Tungurahua Volcano Geopark on 10 April 2025 (with Napo Sumaco, also Ecuador).

9.s:
Match List-A with List-B and select the correct answer using the code given below the lists:

a. Hawaii Island

9.src: APPSC Forest Range Officers Mains General Studies & Mental A
9.x: Hekla – Iceland (b), Kilimanjaro – Tanzania (d), Mauna Loa – Hawaii (a), Krakatoa – Indonesia (c).

9.s: Which of the following volcanoes is NOT active?
9.x: Aconcagua in the Andes is not an active volcano; Cotopaxi, Etna and Stromboli are active.

9.s: In which country is the Popocatepetl volcano, whose magma system was first imaged in 3D, located?

9.s:
Consider the following statements about Hayli Gubbi:
1. It is a shield volcano.
2. It erupted in November 2025 after about 10,000–12,000 years of dormancy.
3. It is a composite volcano.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
9.x: Hayli Gubbi in Ethiopia is a shield volcano that erupted in November 2025 after about 10,000–12,000 years; it is not a composite volcano.

9.s: Volcan de Fuego, which erupted again in June 2026, is associated with the subduction of which plate beneath which other plate?
o: The Nazca Plate beneath the Cocos Plate
The Pacific Plate beneath the Nazca Plate
The Cocos Plate beneath the Caribbean Plate
The Caribbean Plate beneath the Cocos Plate
9.x: The renewed eruption of Guatemala's Volcan de Fuego is associated with the Cocos Plate subducting beneath the Caribbean Plate.
9.tq: Keep the direction of subduction in the correct order: subducting plate first and overriding plate second.
xs: **Volcan de Fuego** (Guatemala) erupts as the **Cocos plate** subducts under the **Caribbean plate** — option **(3)**.
It erupted again in **June 2026**.
xa: **Fuego** is a **composite/stratovolcano** on the **Pacific Ring of Fire**.
First 3D image of Mexico's **Popocatepetl**: magma pools down to **18 km**.
Ring of Fire also has **Fuji, St Helens, Mayon, Dukono**.

9.s: In which country is Kilimanjaro volcano located?
9.x: Kilimanjaro, a rift volcano of the East African Rift, is in Tanzania.

9.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
9.x: Tungurahua is in Ecuador; Hekla is in Iceland, Krakatau in Indonesia and Mauna Loa in Hawaii, USA.

9.s: In which country is White Island (Whakaari), an active volcano, located?
9.x: Whakaari or White Island is an active volcano of New Zealand.

9.s: In which country is the Krakatau volcano located?

**Surface (L)** waves arrive **last** and **cause most damage**.

11.s: Chemical weathering of rocks is much greater in a place with
11.x: Chemical weathering is fastest in hot and humid climates, where heat and abundant water speed up reactions; cold or dry climates slow it.

11.x: Weathering is the natural breaking down and decay of rocks in situ into fine fragments, clays and dissolved matter; it does not involve accumulation or transport.

11.s:
Consider the following statements:

2. Statement-II: Rain water contains carbon dioxide in solution.
