14.s: Which of the following gases traps heat in the atmosphere and contributes most to the greenhouse effect?
14.src: APPSC Forest Beat Officer & Assistant Beat Officer (Mains) P
14.x: Carbon dioxide absorbs outgoing long-wave (infrared) radiation and is the major contributor to the greenhouse effect; O2, N2 and argon do not trap heat.

14.s:
Consider the following statements:
1.
Statement I: The amount of dust particles in the atmosphere is more in subtropical and temperate areas than in equatorial and polar regions.
2. Statement II: Subtropical and temperate areas have less dry winds. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement II explains Statement I
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct but Statement II does not explain Statement I
Statement I is correct but Statement II is not correct
Statement I is not correct, but Statement II is correct
14.x: Dust is more in subtropical and temperate regions than in equatorial and polar regions (I correct) because these areas have MORE dry winds – Statement II ('less dry winds') is wrong.

14.s: The increasing amount of carbon dioxide in the air is slowly raising the temperature of the atmosphere, because it absorbs
o: the water vapour of the air and retains its heat.
the UV part of the solar radiation.
the infrared part of the solar radiation.
14.x: CO2 is transparent to incoming solar radiation but absorbs the outgoing infrared (long-wave) terrestrial radiation, so more CO2 warms the air; it does not absorb UV or all radiation.

14.s: Carbon dioxide is called a greenhouse gas because
o: its concentration remains always higher than other gases.
14.x: CO2 is a greenhouse gas because it absorbs infrared (long-wave) radiation; its share is small and photosynthesis is unrelated.

14.s: Greenhouse effect is the process
o: to obtain suitable temperature for plantation.
of heating the atmosphere by absorption of infrared radiations by atmospheric carbon dioxide.
by which barren mountains changes into green.
in which deep water seems green.
14.x: The greenhouse effect is the heating of the atmosphere as CO2 and other gases absorb outgoing infrared radiation; the other options are nonsense definitions.

14.s: Greenhouse effect is enhanced in the environment due to
14.x: Rising carbon dioxide enhances the greenhouse effect; carbon monoxide is a pollutant but a weak direct GHG, and oxygen is not a GHG.

14.s: In warm, wet tropical regions, up to what share of the atmosphere may water vapour constitute?
14.x: Water vapour may reach 4 per cent in warm, wet tropics and is below 1 per cent in deserts and polar air; it decreases with altitude.
xa: It is the **most abundant greenhouse gas** and decides **air stability**.
It absorbs insolation and keeps in Earth's heat (**blanket effect**).
CO2 and water vapour reach only about **90 km**.

14.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about water vapour in the atmosphere?
o: It absorbs both insolation and terrestrial heat
It is a permanent constituent uniformly distributed at all heights
It influences the stability of the air
14.x: Water vapour is a variable constituent and is not uniformly distributed; it absorbs insolation and terrestrial heat and affects stability.

14.s: In which belts are atmospheric dust particles, mostly found in the lower layers, relatively more abundant?
14.x: Dust is concentrated in the lower atmospheric layers and is more abundant in subtropical and temperate belts, where dry winds help raise and transport particles.
14.tq: Use the distribution comparison rather than the extreme option involving only one belt.
xs: Dust is more abundant in **subtropical and temperate** belts — option **(3)**.
**Dry winds** there lift and carry it; **equatorial and polar** belts have less (option 2).
Dust is concentrated in the **lower layers**, not the thermosphere.
xa: Dust sources: **sea salt, soil, smoke, soot, ash, pollen, meteor dust**.
It acts as **hygroscopic nuclei** for condensation.
Water vapour is **under 1%** in deserts and polar air.

14.s: Which of the following gases are identified as greenhouse gases?
14.x: Methane and nitrous oxide are greenhouse gases that trap outgoing heat. Hydrogen, krypton, neon, helium and argon are not greenhouse gases.
14.tq: Discriminate greenhouse gases from inert gases.
n: Methane and nitrous oxide (N₂O) are greenhouse gases. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
xs: **Methane and nitrous oxide** (N₂O) are **greenhouse gases** — option **(4)**.
The other pairs — **hydrogen**, **krypton**, **neon**, **helium**, **argon** — are **trace** or **inert** gases.
xa: **CO₂** and **water vapour** also contribute to the **greenhouse effect**.
CO₂ is **transparent to incoming sunlight** but **absorbs outgoing terrestrial radiation**.
**CFCs** are potent GHGs — GWP **1,000–23,000**.

14.s: Why do dust particles help in cloud formation?
o: act as hygroscopic nuclei for condensation
14.x: Dust particles serve as hygroscopic nuclei around which water vapour can condense, assisting cloud formation.
14.tq: Link the atmospheric constituent with its specific process-based function.
xs: Dust particles **act as hygroscopic nuclei for condensation** — option **(2)**.
Water vapour condenses around them, forming **clouds**.
xa: Dust is concentrated in the **lower layers**.
More dust in **subtropical and temperate** belts.
Sources include **sea salt** and **meteor dust**.

14.s: Which of the following is the most abundant greenhouse gas in the atmosphere?
14.x: Water vapour (0-4%) is the most abundant greenhouse gas; it absorbs most infrared in the lower atmosphere.

14.s: Which one of the following best explains the greenhouse effect in relation to atmospheric radiation?
o: The atmosphere is transparent to incoming solar radiation but opaque to outgoing terrestrial radiation.
The atmosphere is opaque to incoming solar radiation and transparent to outgoing terrestrial radiation.
The atmosphere absorbs both incoming solar radiation and outgoing terrestrial radiation completely.
The atmosphere reflects all incoming solar radiation and absorbs none of the terrestrial radiation.
14.x: The atmosphere is relatively transparent to incoming solar radiation but absorbs outgoing terrestrial radiation, thereby contributing to the greenhouse effect.
14.tq: Apply the radiation-flow concept by distinguishing incoming solar radiation from outgoing terrestrial radiation.
xs: The atmosphere is **transparent to incoming solar radiation** but **opaque to outgoing terrestrial radiation** — that is the **greenhouse effect**, option **(1)**.
**CO2** is transparent to incoming sunlight but **absorbs outgoing terrestrial radiation**; **water vapour** keeps in earth's heat (**blanket effect**).
The atmosphere neither absorbs all radiation nor reflects all incoming sunlight, so options **(2)-(4)** are wrong.
xa: **Water vapour** is the **most abundant greenhouse gas**; up to **4%** in warm, wet tropics.
CO2 rose **3.5 ppm** to **423.9 ppm** in **2024** — **152%** of pre-industrial (WMO Greenhouse Gas Bulletin 2025).
**CFCs** are about **1,000 times** more heat-absorbent than CO2 and make up **15%** of the enhanced effect.

14.s: Homosphere can be divided into ____ layers.
14.src: APPSC Degree Lecturers General Studies & Mental Ability 2020
14.x: The homosphere (0–~90 km) has three layers – troposphere, stratosphere and mesosphere; the thermosphere and exosphere form the heterosphere.

14.s: Which of the following layer is not included in Homosphere?
14.x: The homosphere comprises the troposphere, stratosphere and mesosphere; the ionosphere belongs to the heterosphere.

14.s: Over which of the following regions is the major ozone hole of the Earth?
14.src: APPSC Assistant Social, BC & Tribal Welfare Officers Screeni
14.x: The ozone hole forms over Antarctica every southern spring, when polar stratospheric clouds help chlorine destroy ozone; the Arctic loss is much smaller. Moved to the atmosphere row.

14.s: The largest ozone hole is observed over
14.src: APPSC Forest Beat Officer & Assistant Beat Officer Screening
14.x: The largest (seasonal) ozone hole lies over Antarctica, not over Africa, Australia or India. Moved to the atmosphere row.

14.s: Which one of the following sequences represents the principal gases of the heterosphere from lower to higher levels, according to molecular weight?
14.x: The heterosphere is described as having nitrogen, atomic oxygen, helium and hydrogen in upward order according to molecular weight.
14.tq: Arrange the gases by the stated upward molecular-weight sequence.
xs: Upward order: **nitrogen, atomic oxygen, helium, hydrogen** — option **(2)**.
In the **heterosphere** gases are layered by **molecular weight**, heaviest lowest.
Option (1) is the reverse order.
xa: The heterosphere lies above **~80-90 km**.
It holds the **thermosphere and exosphere**.
The **homosphere** below has a **uniform** mix of gases.

14.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Homosphere – Gases layered by molecular weight
Heterosphere – Gases layered by molecular weight
14.x: In the heterosphere gases are arranged in layers by molecular weight; the homosphere, below about 80–90 km, has evenly mixed gases.

14.s: Which of the following layers together form the homosphere?
14.x: The homosphere (0 to ~90 km) includes the troposphere, stratosphere and mesosphere; the thermosphere and exosphere form the heterosphere.
14.tq: one-liner

14.s: Up to what height does the homosphere extend from the surface?
14.x: The homosphere, with evenly mixed gases, extends to about 90 km.
14.tq: one-liner

14.s: Which is the main reflector of short-wave radio in the ionosphere?
14.x: The F layer is the main reflector of short-wave radio; the D layer absorbs medium and long waves and the E layer reflects medium-frequency waves.
xa: ⚠ **E** = **Kennelly-Heaviside**; **F** = **Appleton**.
The **D layer** fades at night.
F splits into **F1, F2** by day.

14.s: Which of the following may be disrupted by solar flares and geomagnetic storms?
o: the composition of the homosphere permanently
the formation of all atmospheric dust
14.x: Solar flares and geomagnetic storms can disturb ionospheric conditions and disrupt GNSS signals.
14.tq: Link the space-weather event with its stated communication and navigation effect.
xs: **Solar flares** and **geomagnetic storms** disrupt **GNSS signals** — option **(3)**.
They disturb the **ionosphere**, through which these signals pass.
xa: Indian researchers mapped the **topside ionosphere** up to **1,000 km** for **NavIC/GPS** accuracy.
The ionosphere **reflects radio waves**.
⚠ **E** = Kennelly-Heaviside; **F** = Appleton.

14.s: By which name is the E layer of the ionosphere also known?
14.x: The E layer is the Kennelly-Heaviside layer; the F layer is the Appleton layer.
14.tq: one-liner

14.s: Which ionospheric layer absorbs medium and long waves and fades at night?
14.x: The D layer (60–90 km) absorbs medium/long waves and fades at night.

14.s: By which name is the F layer of the ionosphere also known?
14.x: The F layer is the Appleton layer and is the main reflector of short-wave radio; the E layer is Kennelly-Heaviside.

15.s:
Match the following on heating and cooling of Atmosphere:
List I (Process)

a. Advection

b. Convection

c. Insolation

d. Conduction
List II (Mechanism)

I. Horizontal heating

II. Vertical heating

III. Direct heating

IV. Heating the lower layers
15.x: Advection is horizontal transfer, convection vertical, insolation direct heating and conduction heats the lower air layers touching the ground → a-I, b-II, c-III, d-IV.

15.s: With reference to the Earth's atmosphere, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: The total amount of insolation received at the equator is roughly about 10 times of that received at the
Infrared rays constitute roughly two-thirds of insolation.
Infrared waves are largely absorbed by water vapour that is concentrated in the lower atmosphere.
Infrared waves are a part of the visible spectrum of electromagnetic waves of solar radiation.
15.x: Infra-red waves are largely absorbed by water vapour concentrated in the lower atmosphere (c). The equator gets only ~2.5 times the polar insolation, infra-red is about half (not two-thirds) of insolation and it is not part of the visible spectrum. (UPSC key: c)

15.s: Which one of the following processes is not a part of long-wave radiation?
15.x: Scattering is a short-wave process acting on incoming sunlight; conduction, convection and radiation transfer the long-wave (terrestrial) heat.

15.s: Troposphere is the hottest part of the atmosphere because
o: it is closet to the Sun.
it is heated by the Earth’s surface.
there are charged particles in it.
15.x: The troposphere is heated from below by the Earth's surface (long-wave radiation, conduction), so it is warmest near the ground – not because it is nearer the Sun or generates heat.

15.s: Wind is often found to blow in a hot summer day due to
o: conduction of heat between air and soil on the Earth.
15.x: On a hot day the heated ground warms the air, which rises; cooler air flows in to replace it – a convection current that produces wind.

15.s: Which of the following does not require a medium?
15.x: Radiation transfers heat as electromagnetic waves and needs no medium; conduction and convection need matter.

15.s: Radiations coming from the sun are mostly in the form of
o: Both short and long wavelength infrared.
15.x: Solar radiation is short-wave: mostly visible light plus short-wavelength (near) infra-red. Long-wave infra-red is what the Earth re-emits.

15.s:
Consider the following statements.

I. The Earth receives the Sun’s energy at the infrared end of the spectrum.

II. The Earth re-radiates the Sun’s heat as ultraviolet energy.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
15.x: The Earth receives solar energy mostly as short waves (visible light), not at the infra-red end, and re-radiates it as long-wave infra-red, not ultraviolet → both wrong.

15.s: Which one of the following correctly describes insolation?
o: Vertical transfer of heat by rising air
Horizontal transfer of heat by moving air
Direct heating of the atmosphere by outgoing long-wave radiation
Direct heating by incoming short-wave solar radiation
15.x: Insolation is the direct heating received from incoming short-wave solar radiation.
15.tq: Use the precise mechanism rather than confusing insolation with atmospheric heat transfer.
xs: **Insolation** is **direct heating by incoming short-wave solar radiation** — option **(4)**.
**Vertical** transfer by rising air = **convection**; **horizontal** transfer by moving air = **advection**.
Outgoing long-wave heat is **terrestrial radiation**, the main source that heats the atmosphere.
xa: APPSC-G2 **2023** matched: **Advection - horizontal**, **Convection - vertical**, **Insolation - direct**, **Conduction - lower layers**.
The sun emits **short-wave** radiation; earth re-emits **long-wave infra-red** (**8,000-25,000 nm**).
Planetary **albedo** is about **35%** of insolation.

15.s: What is the horizontal transfer of heat by wind called?
15.x: Advection is the horizontal transfer of heat by wind; vertical transfer by rising warm air is convection.

15.s: The Loo, a hot wind of northern India, is an example of which of the following processes?
15.x: The Loo transfers heat horizontally through moving air and is therefore an example of advection.
15.tq: Identify the direction of movement in the example before naming the process.
xs: The **Loo** of north India is an example of **advection** — **horizontal** transfer of heat by wind — option **(2)**.
**Convection** is vertical transfer; **conduction** heats air in contact with the ground; **radiation** is via electromagnetic waves.
xa: APPSC-G2 **2023** match: **Advection - horizontal**, **Convection - vertical**, **Insolation - direct**, **Conduction - lower layers**.
Convection: heated air becomes **less dense and rises**, cooler air sinks.
**Terrestrial radiation** (long-wave) is the **main source** heating the atmosphere.

15.s: By which of the following is the atmosphere mainly heated?
o: Direct absorption of incoming short-wave solar radiation
Outgoing long-wave terrestrial radiation from below
15.x: The atmosphere is largely transparent to incoming short-wave radiation but absorbs outgoing long-wave terrestrial radiation, so it is heated mainly from below.
xa: ⚠ Trap: "heated more by incoming solar radiation" is **wrong**; greenhouse gases absorb long waves is **right** (UPSC **2024**).
Earth re-emits **long-wave infra-red** (**8,000-25,000 nm**), absorbed by **CO2 and water vapour**.
Without the atmosphere: about **-18 °C** instead of **+15 °C**.

15.s: In what form is terrestrial radiation, the main heater of the atmosphere, emitted?
15.x: The Earth re-emits heat as long-wave infra-red radiation, which heats the air from below.

15.s: Which gases mainly absorb the long-wave radiation re-emitted by the Earth?
15.x: Carbon dioxide and water vapour absorb the Earth's long-wave infra-red radiation.

15.s: Which of the following pairs of heating process and mechanism is correctly matched?
o: Conduction – Heats the lower layers of air
Insolation – Long-wave heat from the Earth
15.x: Conduction heats the lower air in contact with warm ground; advection is horizontal, convection vertical and insolation short-wave.

15.s: Which of the following factor doesn't influence the insolation?
15.x: Insolation depends on latitude (angle of rays), atmospheric transparency and land–sea distribution, but not on longitude.

15.s: The incoming solar radiation is known as:
15.x: Insolation stands for incoming solar radiation – the short-wave solar energy received by the Earth.

15.s: Which parts of the Earth’s surface experience least variation in incoming solar radiation throughout the year?
15.x: Equatorial regions get high-angle rays and near-equal day length all year, so their insolation varies least; seasonal variation increases with latitude.

15.s: The intensity of insolation depends on
15.x: The intensity of insolation depends mainly on the angle of the Sun's rays, which is set by latitude.

15.s: The greatest seasonal contrast of insolation on the Earth is in which of the following latitudinal zones?
15.x: Polar zones have the greatest seasonal contrast – months of continuous daylight in summer and none in winter – whereas the equator is nearly constant.

15.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about insolation?
o: The angle of the Sun's rays affects the insolation received at a place.
The length of the day affects the insolation received at a place.
Atmospheric transparency has no effect on the insolation received.
The slope and aspect of the land affect the insolation received.
15.x: Atmospheric transparency does influence insolation, along with the angle of the rays, duration of sunshine, and slope and aspect of land.

15.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the Earth's aphelion?
15.x: Aphelion occurs around 4 July, when the Earth is approximately 152 million kilometres from the Sun.
15.tq: Use the paired contrast between perihelion and aphelion.
xs: **Aphelion** (Earth farthest from the sun) falls around **4 July** at about **152 million km** — option **(1)**.
Option (2), ~**3 January** at **147 million km**, is **perihelion** (Earth nearest the sun).
xa: ⚠ Perihelion = **Jan**, nearer (**147**); aphelion = **Jul**, farther (**152**) — a common swap trap.
**Earth-sun distance** is one of the factors of insolation, along with **angle of rays** and **length of day**.
The equator receives the **most annual insolation**; the poles the least.

15.s: Why do the highest temperatures on Earth generally occur in the sub-tropical deserts rather than at the Equator?
o: The maximum annual rainfall of the deserts
The permanent presence of cold ocean currents
Persistent cloud cover and humid air
15.x: Sub-tropical deserts around 20°–30° N have clear skies and dry air, permitting very high temperatures; the Equator does not record the highest temperatures merely because it receives strong insolation.
15.tq: Apply the cause-effect relationship instead of choosing the latitude with the strongest general insolation.
xs: Sub-tropical deserts (about **20-30° N**) are hottest because of **clear skies and dry air** — option **(4)**.
Little cloud lets maximum insolation reach the surface; the **equator** has more cloud.
Deserts have scant rainfall, and **cloud cover and humid air** describe the equator, not deserts.
xa: World hottest: **Death Valley**, **56.7°C**; world coldest: **Vostok**, **-89.2°C**.
India coldest: **Dras** (Ladakh), **-45°C** (**1908**).
AP hottest: **Rentachintala** (Palnadu), above **47°C**; AP coldest: **Lambasingi** — the "**Kashmir of AP**".

15.s: At the same latitude, insolation is generally higher over:
o: Polar seas than over tropical land
15.x: Insolation declines towards the poles and, at the same latitude, is higher over continents than over oceans.
xa: The **equator** receives the **most annual insolation**; maximum at the surface is over **subtropical deserts**.
Land heats and cools faster than water — hence the land-sea contrast.
Surplus heat in the **tropics**, deficit towards the **poles**; winds and currents carry heat **poleward**.

15.s: In the Earth's heat budget, where is a heat surplus found?
15.x: The tropics have a heat surplus and the poles a deficit; winds and ocean currents carry heat poleward.
xa: Overall the surface returns all **51** absorbed units, so earth neither warms nor cools.
Oceans took up a record **+23 zettajoules** of heat in **2025** (vs **+16 ZJ** in 2024) = ~**90%** of excess heat.
India's warming is slower partly because of **poleward heat transfer**.

15.s: What type of the Sun's rays does the equator receive, causing it to be heated more than the poles?
15.x: Latitude sets the Sun's angle: the equator gets more direct rays and greater heating, while the poles get oblique rays and lower heating.
n: Latitude is a factor or control of climate. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
The equator receives more direct rays. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
More direct rays at the equator produce greater heating. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
The poles receive oblique rays. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Oblique rays at the poles produce lower heating. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Seasonal variation increases with latitude. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Annual temperature range is generally greater toward higher latitudes. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xa: Annual range is **minimum at the equator**.
The **equator** receives the **most annual insolation**; the **poles** the least.
**Perihelion** ~**3 Jan**, **147 million km**; **aphelion** ~**4 Jul**, **152 million km**.

15.s: On about which date is the Earth at perihelion, its closest point to the Sun?
15.x: Perihelion falls around 3 January (about 147 million km); aphelion around 4 July.

15.s: What is the approximate Earth–Sun distance at perihelion?
15.x: The Earth is about 147 million km from the Sun at perihelion and about 152 million km at aphelion.

15.s: How does insolation received at the Earth's surface generally change from the Equator towards the poles?
15.x: The Equator gets direct rays and the poles oblique rays, so insolation falls poleward.

15.s: Which among the following has the highest albedo?
15.x: Fresh snow has the highest albedo (75–95%), far above sand, grass or water (below 10%).

15.s: Which among the following has the highest albedo? ma (Da
15.x: Fresh snow reflects most incoming sunlight – the highest albedo; oceans and forests absorb far more.

15.s: Which one of the following reflects back more sunlight as compared to the other three?
15.x: Land covered with fresh snow reflects the most sunlight (albedo up to 75–95%); desert sand, cropland and prairie reflect much less.

15.s: Which one of the following is associated with 'Albedo'?
15.x: Albedo is the reflecting power of a surface – the fraction of incoming radiation it reflects.

15.s: Which one of the following reflects more sunlight as compared to the three?
15.x: Fresh snow has the highest albedo of the four and reflects the most sunlight.

15.s: Nearly 30% of the solar radiations return back to the space without contributing anything to the Earth’s surface temperature. This amount of radiation is known as
15.x: The share of insolation reflected straight back to space (about 30–35 units of 100) is the Earth's (planetary) albedo; it does not heat the surface.

15.s: Without green house effect, the average temperature of earth’s surface would be
15.x: Without the greenhouse effect the Earth's average surface temperature would be about −18°C instead of about +15°C.

15.s: If the Earth did not have an atmosphere, temperature extremes between day and night would
15.x: Without an atmosphere there would be no greenhouse blanket: days would heat unchecked and nights would lose heat rapidly, so day–night extremes would increase.

15.s: According to recent assessments (Apr 2025), the Arctic is warming at about what rate compared with the global average?
15.x: The Arctic has warmed by at least 2 deg C and is warming 3-4 times faster than the global average (older estimates said about twice), driven by the ice-albedo feedback in which melting ice exposes dark ocean. It is not slower, equal or ten times faster.
xs: The Arctic is warming about **3-4 times faster** than the global average (Apr **2025**) — option **(1)**.
It has warmed at least **2°C**; older notes said about **twice** as fast.
Driver: the **ice-albedo feedback** — melting ice exposes dark ocean that absorbs more heat.
xa: **Black carbon** on snow cuts albedo, adding to warming.
Global land temperature is up **1.59 °C** since pre-industrial (UNEP Emissions Gap **2025**).
India's annual mean is up **0.7 °C** since **1900**; slower partly because of **Arctic amplification** and aerosol masking.

15.s: After fresh snow, which of the following surfaces has the highest albedo?
15.x: The descending albedo order is fresh snow, sand, grass, forest and water, so sand comes second.

15.s: Which clouds tend to reflect incoming sunlight and produce cooling?
15.x: Low, thick clouds reflect more sunlight and cause cooling, whereas high, thin clouds tend to trap outgoing heat.
xa: ⚠ **High thin = warming; low thick = cooling**.
Of 100 units of insolation, clouds reflect **27**; total reflected **35** (planetary albedo).
**Clear nights** lose more heat; **cloudy nights** stay warmer as clouds send heat back.

15.s: What does the albedo of a surface refer to?
o: share of incoming radiation reflected by the surface
amount of heat stored below the surface
rate at which terrestrial radiation is emitted
amount of moisture absorbed by the surface
15.x: Albedo is the proportion or share of incoming radiation that a surface reflects.
15.tq: Use the exact definition and distinguish reflection from absorption and emission.
xs: **Albedo** is the **share of incoming radiation a surface reflects** — option **(1)**.
Heat storage, emission of terrestrial radiation and moisture absorption are not albedo.
xa: Ranking: **fresh snow** (highest, APPSC-G1 **2019**) > sand > grass > forest > water.
Fresh snow **80-90%**; water (sun high) **below 10%**.
**Planetary albedo** ≈ **35%** (35 of 100 units).
**Black carbon** on snow cuts albedo; melting ice exposes dark ocean (**ice-albedo feedback**).

15.s: Why can melting of ice intensify warming?
o: converts long-wave radiation into short-wave radiation
increases the albedo of the exposed ocean
exposes a darker ocean surface that absorbs more heat
prevents the ocean from absorbing solar radiation
15.x: Melting ice exposes dark ocean water, which has a lower albedo and absorbs more heat, producing a positive ice-albedo feedback.
15.tq: Trace the cause-effect chain from surface change to albedo, absorption and warming.
xs: Melting ice **exposes a darker ocean surface that absorbs more heat** — option **(3)** — the **ice-albedo feedback**.
Dark water has **lower albedo** (**below 10%**) than ice and snow (**80-90%**), so it does not raise albedo or stop absorption.
xa: The Arctic has warmed at least **2°C** and warms **3-4 times** faster than the global average (Apr **2025**).
**Black carbon** on snow also cuts albedo.
Albedo ranking: **fresh snow** > sand > grass > forest > **water**.

15.s: What effect do high, thin clouds generally have?
o: Raise the Earth's albedo the most
15.x: High, thin clouds trap heat (warming), while low, thick clouds reflect sunlight (cooling).

15.s: What is the approximate albedo of fresh snow?
15.x: Fresh snow reflects 75–95% of incoming radiation; dry sand 20–40%, crop land 15–25% and water below 10%.

15.s: Which of the following pairs about the 35 units of insolation reflected to space is correctly matched?
15.x: Of the 35 reflected units, clouds reflect 27, scattering 6 and snow and ice 2.

15.s: Of 100 units of insolation reaching the top of the atmosphere, how many are absorbed by the Earth's surface?
15.x: Of 100 units, 35 are reflected to space, 14 absorbed by the atmosphere and 51 by the Earth's surface.

15.s: Of the 51 units absorbed by the Earth's surface, how many are radiated directly to space?
15.x: The surface radiates 17 units directly to space and 34 to the atmosphere.

15.s: Of 100 units of insolation, how many are absorbed by the atmosphere?
15.x: Of 100 units, 35 are reflected, 14 absorbed by the atmosphere and 51 by the surface.

15.s: What do the 35 units of insolation reflected back to space form?
15.x: The 35 units reflected by clouds, scattering and snow and ice make up the planetary albedo.

15.s: In the Earth's heat budget, how many units does the atmosphere radiate to space?
15.x: The atmosphere sends 48 units (14 + 34) to space; with 17 from the surface, 65 units go out.

15.s: Carbon dioxide contributes approximately what share of the greenhouse effect?
15.x: CO2 contributes about 60%, from fossil fuels, deforestation and cement; methane about 20%, CFCs about 15% and N2O about 5%.
xa: **Water vapour** is the most abundant greenhouse gas (a feedback).
Without the atmosphere the surface would be about **-18 °C** instead of **+15 °C**.

15.s: Which one of the following gases is the most abundant greenhouse gas and acts importantly as a feedback in the climate system?
15.x: Water vapour is the most abundant greenhouse gas and functions importantly as a climate feedback.
15.tq: Distinguish abundance from the percentage contribution estimates of the other gases.
xs: **Water vapour** is the **most abundant greenhouse gas** and acts as a **feedback** — option **(1)**.
**CO2** has the largest share (~**60%**) among listed gases; **methane** ~**20%**; **N2O** ~**5%**.
xa: Greenhouse gases: **CO2, CH4, water vapour, N2O** trap heat (APPSC **2025**).
Earth's long-wave radiation is absorbed by **CO2 and water vapour**.
Without the atmosphere: about **-18 °C** instead of **+15 °C**.

15.s: With carbon dioxide assigned a Global Warming Potential of 1 over 100 years, which of the following ranges is correctly matched?
15.x: On the stated 100-year scale, carbon dioxide has a GWP of 1, methane 28–36 and nitrous oxide 265–298.
15.tq: Keep the gases and their ranges in the correct order and avoid reversing methane with nitrous oxide.
xs: With CO2 = **1**, **methane 28-36** and **N2O 265-298** (100-year GWP) — option **(1)**.
Option (4) swaps the two ranges; N2O is far more potent per unit than methane.
xa: ⚠ Older table: methane **21**, N2O **310**.
Shares of the greenhouse effect: **CO2 ~60%**, **methane ~20%**, **CFCs ~15%**, **N2O ~5%**.
N2O sources: **fertilisers**, burning coal/biomass; methane: **paddy, wetlands, livestock, landfills**.

15.s: In the absence of the atmosphere, what would be the approximate average surface temperature of the Earth?
15.x: Without the atmospheric heat-trapping effect, the average surface temperature would be about −18°C rather than approximately +15°C.
15.tq: Distinguish the observed average from the estimated no-atmosphere value.
xs: Without the atmosphere, the surface would be about **-18 °C instead of +15 °C** — option **(3)**.
Trapped heat from **greenhouse gases** keeps the average temperature up (UPSC **2025**: all three statements correct).
Option (4) reverses the two figures.
xa: Atmosphere is **transparent to short-wave** sunlight, **opaque to long-wave** terrestrial radiation.
Greenhouse gases: **CO2, CH4, water vapour, N2O** (APPSC **2025**).
Global land temperature up **1.59 °C** since pre-industrial (UNEP Emissions Gap **2025**).

15.s: Methane contributes approximately what share of the greenhouse effect?
15.x: Methane gives about 20% of the greenhouse effect; CO₂ about 60%, CFCs about 15% and N₂O about 5%.

15.s:
Consider the following statements about the greenhouse effect:
1. The atmosphere is transparent to short-wave sunlight.
2. The atmosphere is transparent to long-wave terrestrial radiation.
3. Without the atmosphere, the Earth's average surface temperature would be about −18°C.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
15.x: The atmosphere lets short-wave sunlight through but is opaque to long-wave terrestrial radiation; without it the Earth would be about −18°C.

15.s: Which greenhouse gas is known as 'marsh gas'?
15.x: Methane, called marsh gas, comes from paddy fields, wetlands and livestock and gives about 20% of the greenhouse effect.

15.s: According to the UNEP Emissions Gap Report 2025, by how much has global land temperature risen since pre-industrial times?
15.x: The UNEP Emissions Gap Report 2025 puts the rise in global land temperature at 1.59°C above pre-industrial levels.

15.s: Cloudy nights are warmer compared to clear cloudless nights, because clouds:
o: prevent cold waves from the sky from descending on Earth
reflect back heat given off by Earth
produce heat and radiate it towards Earth
absorb heat from the atmosphere and send it towards Earth
15.x: Clouds absorb and reflect back the long-wave heat given off by the Earth, so cloudy nights stay warmer than clear nights.

15.s: In which part of India is the daily range of temperature highest?
15.x: Desert areas of Rajasthan have the highest daily range of temperature – hot days, cold nights under clear dry skies; coasts and islands are equable.

15.s: The average annual temperature of a meteorological station is 26oC, its average annual rainfall is 63 cm and the annual range temperature is 9oC. The station in question is:
15.x: A mean of ~26°C with an annual range of only ~9°C fits Chennai, a tropical coastal station; Allahabad has a large range, Cherrapunji far more rain and Kolkata a cooler winter. (UPSC key: b)

15.s: Clear sky nights are cooler than cloudy sky nights due to
15.x: On clear nights the Earth's heat escapes freely by radiation, with no cloud blanket to return it, so they are cooler than cloudy nights.

15.s: Cloudy nights are warmer than clear nights because
o: it acts as a hindrance to terrestrial radiation
15.x: Clouds hinder outgoing terrestrial (long-wave) radiation and send it back like a blanket, so cloudy nights stay warmer; ozone depletion and 'isolation' are irrelevant.

15.s: Clear nights are colder than cloudy nights because of ………
15.x: On clear nights terrestrial radiation escapes freely to space, so they are colder; the cause is radiation loss, not conduction or condensation.

15.s: Which sky condition produces the greatest terrestrial cooling at night?
15.x: Clear skies allow more daytime solar heating and more night-time terrestrial cooling, whereas clouds cut both.
n: Cloudy conditions reduce incoming solar radiation during the day. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cloudy conditions produce cooler daytime temperatures. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Clear skies allow greater solar heating during the day. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Clear skies cause greater terrestrial cooling at night. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cloud cover affects day and night temperature. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xa: **Cloudy nights** stay warmer.
Annual range is **minimum at the equator**; largest in high-latitude interiors (**Siberia**).
Seasonal differences are **maximum in high latitudes** (APPSC-G1 **2023**).

15.s: Which one of the following regions of India records the highest diurnal range of temperature in winter?
15.x: The diurnal range is highest in north-western India during winter, where it is about 14°–18°C.
15.tq: Identify the correct region before matching it with the associated numerical range.
xs: Winter diurnal range is highest in **north-western India** — **14-18°C** — option **(3)**.
Coasts and deltas have a **small range** due to sea moderation.
xa: **Continentality** gives large annual and daily ranges in northern interiors of India.
**Clear nights** lose more heat — cold nights and frost.
India coldest: **Dras** (Ladakh), **-45°C** (**1908**).

15.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Temperature generally decreases from the equator towards the poles.
The sea moderates temperature, making coastal climates more equable.
Interior areas generally have a smaller annual temperature range than coastal areas.
Temperature generally decreases with increasing altitude.
15.x: Option C is incorrect: interior areas have a larger annual range, because land heats and cools fast. Coasts are equable because the sea moderates them.
n: Temperature generally decreases from the equator toward the poles. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Temperature generally decreases with increasing altitude. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
The sea moderates temperature. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Coastal climates are equable. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Interior temperatures are more extreme. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Coastal regions have a smaller annual temperature range. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Interior regions have a larger annual temperature range. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **interior areas** have a **smaller annual temperature range** than **coastal areas** — option **(3)**: interiors have a **larger** range.
**Land heats and cools rapidly**, while the **sea heats and cools slowly** and **moderates temperature** — so coasts are **equable**, interiors **extreme (continental)**.
The others are correct: temperature **decreases toward the poles** and **with altitude**.
xa: **Warm currents raise** coastal temperatures; **cold currents lower** them.
The **annual range** is generally **greater toward higher latitudes**.
**Hottest latitudes:** **subtropical deserts** (about **20–30° N**), not the equator.

15.s: Where is the annual range of temperature largest?
o: High-latitude continental interiors such as Siberia
15.x: The annual range is largest in high-latitude continental interiors like Siberia and minimum at the equator; coasts have a small range.
xa: **Seasonal differences are maximum in high latitudes** (APPSC-G1 **2023**).
**Continentality** = large annual and daily ranges (northern interiors of India).
AP: coast low diurnal range; **Rayalaseema** high.

15.s: Where in Andhra Pradesh is a high diurnal range of temperature found?
15.x: The coast has a low diurnal range moderated by the sea and sea breezes (as at Visakhapatnam and Kakinada), while interior Rayalaseema has a high range.
xa: Coasts are **equable/maritime**, moderated by the sea; interiors show **continentality**.
AP hottest: **Rentachintala** (Palnadu), above **47°C**; AP coldest: **Lambasingi**.
**48.1 °C** at **Piduguralla** (Palnadu) on **21 May 2026**.

15.s: Where is the annual range of temperature minimum?
15.x: The annual range is smallest at the Equator and largest in high-latitude continental interiors such as Siberia.

15.s: Where is the seasonal range of temperature maximum?
15.x: Seasonal range is maximum in high latitudes (APPSC-G1 2023) and minimum at the Equator.

15.s: The January isotherm taken as a basis for dividing India into tropical and sub-tropical zones is
15.x: The January 18°C isotherm divides India into the tropical south and the sub-tropical north.

15.s:
Consider the following statements
1.
Statement I: In January, in the Northern Hemisphere, the isotherms bend equatorward while crossing the landmasses, and poleward while crossing the oceans.
2. Statement II: In January, the air over the oceans is warmer than that over the landmasses in the Northern Hemisphere. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement II explains Statement I
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct but Statement II does not explain Statement I
Statement I is correct, but Statement II is not correct
Statement I is not correct, but Statement II is correct
15.x: In the NH January, oceans are warmer than land, so isotherms bend equatorward over the cold continents and poleward over the warm oceans – both true and II explains I. (UPSC 2025 key: a)

15.s: The highest temperature on the earth is recorded at -
15.x: The highest temperatures are recorded not at the Equator (cloudy, humid) but in the subtropical deserts around 20° N (clear skies, dry air).

15.s: The thermal equator is found
o: both North and South of geographical equator.
15.x: The thermal equator lies mostly north of the geographical equator because the NH has more land, which heats more.

15.s: Why does temperature normally decrease with increasing altitude?
o: Higher air receives more long-wave radiation from the Sun.
The ground heats the air from below, while higher air is thinner and contains less water vapour and dust.
The Earth stops emitting radiation above the lower atmosphere.
The atmosphere is heated mainly from above by direct solar radiation.
15.x: The ground heats the atmosphere from below. At higher levels the air is thinner and contains less water vapour and dust, so it absorbs less heat.
15.tq: Identify the heating source and the properties of higher air.
xs: The **ground heats the air from below**, while higher air is **thinner** with **less water vapour and dust** — option **(2)**.
So higher air absorbs less heat, and temperature falls at the normal lapse rate of **6.5 °C/km**.
The atmosphere is not heated mainly from above by direct sunlight, and the earth does not stop emitting radiation.
xa: The sun emits **short-wave**; earth re-emits **long-wave infra-red** (**8,000-25,000 nm**), absorbed by CO2 and water vapour.
**Temperature inversion** is when this reverses and temperature **rises** with height.
**Terrestrial radiation** is the main source heating the atmosphere.

15.s: Which climatic control explains why the Himalayas are cooler despite their lower latitude?
15.x: Altitude makes the Himalayas cool despite their low latitude, since temperature falls about 6.5°C per km.
15.tq: Recall the effect of each climatic control.
n: Altitude is a factor or control of climate. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Temperature generally decreases with increasing altitude. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
The Himalayas are cooler despite having a lower latitude. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xs: **Altitude** explains it — option **(1)**: temperature **decreases with increasing altitude**, so the **Himalayas** are **cooler despite a lower latitude**.
**Distance from sea** moderates range; **ocean currents** raise or lower coastal temperatures; **cloud cover** modifies day and night heating.
xa: Normal lapse rate **6.5 °C/km**.
Higher air is **thinner**, with **less water vapour and dust**, so it absorbs less heat.
Air is heated **from below** by terrestrial radiation.

15.s: What is the normal lapse rate, at which temperature falls with increasing height in the troposphere?
15.x: Temperature normally falls with height at about 6.5 °C per km, because the air is heated from below and higher air absorbs less heat.
15.tq: Normal lapse = 6.5 per km (about 1 °C per 165 m).
xs: The normal lapse rate is about **6.5 °C per km** — option **(3)**.
Air is heated **from below**; higher air is thinner with less water vapour and dust, so it absorbs less heat.
xa: **Convection** (vertical transfer by rising warm air) is **confined to the troposphere**.
In a **temperature inversion**, temperature **rises** with height instead.
The stratosphere is a **permanent inversion** layer.

15.s: Which of the following is NOT a reason why temperature falls with height in the troposphere?
o: The air is heated from below by the ground.
Higher air holds less water vapour and dust.
Higher air is heated directly by the Sun more than lower air.
15.x: Air is heated from below, not directly by the Sun; thinner air with less vapour and dust aloft makes temperature fall with height.

15.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about factors affecting temperature?
o: Cold ocean currents raise coastal temperatures.
Continentality produces extreme interior climates with a large annual range.
Cloud cover reduces daytime heating and night-time cooling.
Warm ocean currents raise coastal temperatures.
15.x: Cold ocean currents lower coastal temperatures and favour west-coast deserts; it is warm currents that raise them.
n: Distance from the sea or continentality is a factor or control of climate. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Interior climates are extreme. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cloud cover modifies heating and cooling. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Warm ocean currents raise coastal temperatures. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cold ocean currents lower coastal temperatures. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Relief alters temperature and air movement. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Mountain slopes and aspects affect temperature. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cold currents combined with subtropical highs are often associated with arid west-coast climates. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cloud cover affects day and night temperature. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xa: Continental interiors have **large annual and daily ranges** — hot summers, cold winters.
**Cloudy nights** stay warmer; **clear nights** lose more heat.
**Relief** alters **temperature** and **air movement**.

15.s: How do isotherms in the Northern Hemisphere bend in January?
o: Equatorward over both land and oceans
Poleward over land and equatorward over oceans
Equatorward over land and poleward over oceans
15.x: In January, Northern Hemisphere isotherms bend equatorward over colder landmasses and poleward over relatively warmer oceans.
xa: **Isotherms** join places of equal temperature, running roughly **east-west**.
Southern Hemisphere isotherms are **more regular** (mostly ocean).
**Thermal equator** lies mostly **north of the equator** (more land in the NH).

15.s: In winter, India's 20°C isotherm runs approximately from the mouth of the Tapi to which delta?
15.x: In winter the 20°C isotherm runs from the Tapi mouth to the Mahanadi delta; temperature rises from north to south.
xa: In **January**, isotherms bend **equatorward over land** and **poleward over oceans** (UPSC **2025**).
The **thermal equator** lies mostly **north of the equator** (more land in the NH).
India's winter **diurnal range** is highest in the north-west — **14–18°C**.

15.s: Which of the following defines the thermal equator?
o: line joining places of highest mean temperature, generally lying north of the geographical Equator.
boundary between the tropical and polar zones, fixed at 23½° latitude.
line joining the coldest places in both hemispheres.
geographical Equator, which never shifts seasonally.
15.x: The thermal equator is the line of highest mean temperature. It lies mostly north of the geographical Equator and shifts with the apparent movement of the Sun.
15.tq: Distinguish the shifting thermal equator from the fixed geographical Equator.
xs: The **thermal equator** is the line of **highest mean temperature**, lying mostly **north of the geographical equator** — option **(1)**.
It lies north because the **NH has more land**, and it **shifts** with the sun's apparent movement — so it is not fixed.
xa: **Isotherms** run roughly east-west; in January they bend **equatorward over land**.
Southern Hemisphere isotherms are **more regular** (mostly ocean).
Annual range is **minimum at the equator**.

15.s: What are lines joining places having equal temperature called?
15.x: Isotherms join places of equal temperature; they generally run east-west and are more regular in the ocean-dominated Southern Hemisphere.
xa: January: isotherms bend **equatorward over land**, **poleward over oceans**; July reverses.
**Thermal equator** = line of highest mean temperature, mostly north of the equator.
India winter: **20°C isotherm** runs from the **Tapti** mouth to the **Mahanadi delta**.

15.s: How do isotherms in the Northern Hemisphere bend in July?
o: Equatorward over land and poleward over oceans
Poleward over both land and oceans
Equatorward over both land and oceans
Poleward over land and equatorward over oceans
15.x: In July isotherms bend poleward over land and the reverse over oceans; January shows the opposite pattern.

15.s: Why are isotherms more regular in the Southern Hemisphere?
o: Closer to the Sun in July
15.x: The Southern Hemisphere is mostly ocean, so its isotherms run more regularly east-west.

15.s: What does the Northern Hemisphere have that makes the thermal equator lie mostly north of the Equator?
15.x: The thermal equator, the line of highest mean temperature, lies mostly north of the Equator because there is more land there.

15.s: Which January isotherm divides India into tropical and sub-tropical parts?
15.x: The January 18°C isotherm separates tropical south India from sub-tropical north India.

15.s: In a valley inversion, why is the valley floor colder than the slopes?
o: warm air flows downslope and accumulates at the valley floor.
the valley floor is always nearer to the Sun.
cold air drains downslope and settles in the valley.
the slopes receive no solar radiation in winter.
15.x: Cold, dense air flows downslope and accumulates in valleys, producing frost pockets while the slopes remain relatively warmer.
15.tq: Follow the movement of dense cold air to determine the colder location.
xs: In a **valley inversion**, **cold air drains downslope** and settles in the valley — option **(3)**.
This creates **frost pockets** on valley floors while **slopes stay warmer**.
xa: Hence **orchards/plantations** are placed on **upper slopes**.
It is also called **air-drainage inversion**.
Other types: **ground/radiation**, **frontal/advection**, **permanent** (polar areas).

15.s: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Frontal inversion — association with a frontal boundary
Valley inversion — downslope drainage of cold air
Surface or radiation inversion — night-time cooling of the ground
Stratosphere — absence of any inversion condition
15.x: The stratosphere is a permanent inversion layer, so it is incorrect to associate it with the absence of inversion.
15.tq: Find the single reversed or denied relationship in the list.
xs: **Stratosphere — absence of any inversion** is wrongly matched — option **(4)**.
The **stratosphere** is a **permanent inversion layer**; permanent inversions also occur in **polar areas**.
Others are correct: **frontal** inversion at fronts; **valley** = cold-air drainage; **ground/radiation** = night cooling.
xa: Inversion conditions: **long winter nights, clear skies, calm dry air, snow cover**.
Effects: **fog, frost, smog**.
Valley inversion → **frost pockets** on floors, orchards on upper slopes.

15.s: What is a condition in which temperature rises with height instead of falling called?
15.x: In a temperature inversion the normal lapse rate reverses; it is favoured by long winter nights, clear skies and calm dry air.
xa: Types: **ground/radiation**, **valley (air-drainage)**, **frontal/advection**, **permanent** (polar areas).
Effects: **fog**, **frost**, **smog**; pollutants trapped in the boundary layer.
Valley inversion makes **frost pockets** on valley floors — orchards go on **upper slopes**.

15.s: Fog, frost, smog and the trapping of pollutants in the planetary boundary layer are effects of which condition?
15.x: Temperature inversions can produce fog, frost and smog and trap pollutants within the planetary boundary layer.
xa: Conditions: **long winter nights, clear skies, calm dry air, snow cover**.
**Valley inversion**: cold air drains downslope → **frost pockets** on valley floors; **orchards** on upper slopes.
Permanent inversion: **polar areas**; the **stratosphere** is a permanent inversion layer.

15.s: Which layer of the atmosphere is a permanent inversion layer?
15.x: The stratosphere is the permanent inversion layer, where temperature rises with height.

15.s: Which of the following does NOT favour a temperature inversion?
15.x: Inversions need long winter nights, clear skies, calm dry air and snow cover; cloudy skies do not favour them.

15.s: In valleys with temperature inversion, why are orchards usually planted on upper slopes?
o: Frost pockets form on the valley floor
Valley floors are warmer at night
Upper slopes are colder at night
15.x: Cold air drains into the valley floor and forms frost pockets, while the slopes stay warmer.

15.s: In absorption of insolation, the most significant part is played by
15.x: Of the options, carbon dioxide (with water vapour, not offered) absorbs the most insolation over a broad band; ozone absorbs only a small share (UV), and oxygen and haze little. Moved to insolation and heat budget.

15.s:
Consider the following statements:

16.s: Which one of the following statements regarding local winds is correct?
o: They are temporary, predictable and region-specific winds caused by local temperature and pressure differences.

16.x: Local winds are temporary, predictable and region-specific. They arise from factors such as differential heating, pressure gradients, relief, surface cover and season.
16.tq: Distinguish local winds from planetary and seasonal winds by scale and cause.
xs: Local winds are **temporary, predictable and region-specific**, caused by **local temperature and pressure differences** — option **(1)**.
Causes: **differential heating**, **pressure gradient**, **relief**, **surface cover**, **season** — so they are not unrelated to relief.
Permanent winds driven by the Earth's rotation are the **planetary winds**; a seasonal reversal over the subcontinent is the **monsoon**.
xa: Indian pre-monsoon local storms: **Nor'westers / Kaal Baisakhi** (east), **"aandhi"** (north-west), **Mango showers** (south).
**Loo**: hot, dry, dusty summer afternoon wind of the north plains and **Rayalaseema**.
⚠ **Foehn** = Alps; **Chinook** = Rockies.

16.s: Which pressure belt is associated with sinking dry air and hot deserts?
16.x: The subtropical high has sinking dry air and hot deserts; the equatorial low has calm rising air and the polar high cold sinking air.
xa: Latitudes: equatorial low **0-5°**, subtropical high **30-35°**, subpolar low **~60-65°**, polar high **90°**.
Other names: equatorial low = **Doldrums/ITCZ**; subtropical high = **Horse latitudes**.

16.s: Following the overhead sun, by about how much do the pressure belts shift seasonally?
16.x: The belts shift about 5°–10° north in the NH summer and south in winter, not 25°–30°.
xa: In NH summer the **ITCZ** shifts north over the Indian plains (**monsoon trough**) — this drives the monsoon.
In winter the ITCZ migrates **south of India** → **north-east monsoon**.
Southward shift of the doldrums → heavy rain in **southern states** (**bimodal rainfall**).

16.s: Which of the following describes the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone?
o: A high-pressure zone near the poles where polar easterlies diverge
A low-pressure zone at 60°–65° where polar highs converge
A high-pressure zone at 30°–35° where westerlies originate
A low-pressure zone near the Equator where the trade winds converge
16.x: The ITCZ is the equatorial low-pressure zone formed where the trade winds from the two hemispheres converge.

xs: The ITCZ is **a low-pressure zone near the Equator where the trade winds converge** — option **(4)**.
**ITCZ** = **Inter Tropical Convergence Zone**, the **equatorial low** (doldrums).
**30-35°** is the subtropical high and **60-65°** the subpolar low — not the ITCZ.
xa: Asked in **APPSC 2019** and **APPSC-GS 2019**.
In NH summer the ITCZ shifts north over the Indian plains as the **monsoon trough**.
The **modern monsoon theory (1957)** is built on the **northward shift of the ITCZ**.

16.s: At about which latitudes does the subpolar low-pressure belt lie?
16.x: The subpolar low lies at about 60–65°, where the westerlies meet the polar easterlies.

16.s: In which direction do the pressure belts shift during the Northern Hemisphere summer?
16.x: The belts follow the overhead sun, moving north in the NH summer and south in winter.

Decreased air density produces low pressure. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]

16.s: What do closely spaced isobars on a weather map indicate?
o: A gentle pressure gradient and calm air
A steep pressure gradient and strong winds
Air moving from low to high pressure

xa: **Isobars** join places of **equal pressure**, reduced to **sea level**.

16.x: Standard sea-level pressure is 1013.25 mb (hPa).
xa: **Pressure gradient** = fall of pressure per unit distance → sets **wind speed** (**APPSC-G2 2011**).
**Closely spaced isobars** = steep gradient = **strong wind**.
Barometer (**mercury**, **aneroid**) and **barograph** measure pressure in **millibar/hectopascal**.

xs: **Anemometer — wind speed** is correctly matched — option **(2)**.
**Barometer** and **barograph** measure **pressure**, not wind direction or rainfall.
**Wind vane** shows **wind direction**, not atmospheric pressure.
xa: ⚠ **Anemometer** = speed; **wind vane** = direction.
Wind speed is given in **km/h** or **knots**; pressure in **millibar/hectopascal**.
Barometer types: **mercury** and **aneroid**; the **barograph** records pressure continuously.

16.x: Isobars join places of equal pressure; closely spaced isobars show a steep pressure gradient and strong winds.

16.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Sub-Tropical Westerly Jet over India?
o: It lies north of the Himalayas in winter and south of them in summer.
It remains north of the Himalayas throughout the year.
It remains south of the Himalayas throughout the year.
It lies south of the Himalayas in winter and shifts north of them in summer.
16.x: The Sub-Tropical Westerly Jet lies south of the Himalayas in winter and shifts north of them in summer.
16.tq: Test the seasonal reversal and location of a closely associated jet stream.
xs: The **STJ** lies **south of the Himalayas in winter** and shifts **north of them in summer** — option **(4)**.
Options (1), (2) and (3) reverse or freeze this seasonal shift.

16.s: During which season is the polar vortex, a cold low-pressure region around the poles, strongest?
16.x: The polar vortex exists year-round, is strongest in winter, and its anticlockwise flow keeps cold air near the poles.
xa: A **strong vortex** keeps the cold air up north and warm air to the south (**APPSC 2018**; **APPSC-GS 2018**).
Layers: tropospheric up to **15 km**; stratospheric **15-50 km** (seasonal).
**Sudden stratospheric warming** / **Rossby waves** weaken it → cold air spills into mid-latitudes.

16.s: In which month does the Sub-Tropical Westerly Jet return over India, marking the end of the monsoon?
16.x: The Sub-Tropical Westerly Jet withdraws before the monsoon burst and returns in October as the monsoon ends.
xa: STJ lies **south of the Himalayas in winter**, **north** in summer.
Western disturbances come from the **Mediterranean**; they worsened extremes in the **2026** monsoon.
⚠ **STJ** = westerly, winter; **TEJ** = easterly, summer.

**Somali (Findlater) Jet**: low-level, off the **East African coast**, intensifies monsoon winds.

16.s: What is the Somali (Findlater) Jet?
o: Low-level jet off the East African coast
Upper-level easterly jet over the Indian plains
Sub-tropical westerly jet carrying western disturbances

xa: The **TEJ** (**5-20°N**) runs from the South China Sea to **East Africa** and strengthens the SW monsoon.
The **STJ** carries **western disturbances**; its withdrawal lets the monsoon burst.
Jet streams in general blow at **10-12 km**.

xa: The STJ lies **south of the Himalayas in winter**, **north** in summer.
Its **withdrawal** lets the monsoon **"burst"**; it **returns in October** to end it.

16.s: Who first identified jet streams in the 1920s?
16.x: Wasaburo Ooishi of Japan first identified jet streams in the 1920s; they became widely known during the Second World War.
xa: **Sub-Tropical Westerly Jet (STJ)** lies south of the Himalayas in **winter**, carries **western disturbances**; shifts **north of the Himalayas** in summer.
**Tropical Easterly Jet (TEJ)**: summer only, **5-20°N**, **strengthens the SW monsoon**.
**Somali (Findlater) Jet** is a **low-level** jet off the **East African coast**.
⚠ **STJ** = westerly, winter; **TEJ** = easterly, summer.

16.s: What may happen when Rossby waves weaken the polar vortex?
o: The vortex becomes permanently stationary and cold air remains confined to the poles.

The polar region changes into a high-pressure warm region throughout the year.

xs: **The winds may reverse, the vortex may split and cold air may spill into the mid-latitudes** — option **(4)**.
**Rossby waves** or **sudden stratospheric warming** weaken the vortex → **cold spells** in mid-latitudes.
A strong vortex, not a weakened one, keeps cold air confined to the poles.
xa: The vortex's **anticlockwise flow** locks cold air near the poles (**APPSC 2018**).
It is a **low-pressure, cold-air** reservoir, strongest in **winter**.
Tropospheric part to **15 km**; stratospheric part **15-50 km**.

The low pressure conditions in North-West India.

16.x: Trade winds belong to the Hadley cell, a thermal convection circulation: air rises at the equator and surface air flows in from the subtropical highs.

16.x: Trade winds blow from the subtropical high (horse latitudes) to the equatorial low; westerlies go poleward and doldrums are a calm belt.

16.x: Trade winds are planetary (permanent) winds; monsoon is periodic and Chinook and Mistral are local winds.

16.s: Where is the Coriolis force maximum?
16.x: The Coriolis force is zero at the equator and maximum at the poles; it is proportional to wind speed.

16.s: Which one of the following statements regarding friction is NOT correct?
o: It is negligible in the upper air.
It increases the speed of surface winds.
It is stronger over land than over a smooth water surface.
16.x: Friction slows surface winds; it is stronger over land and becomes negligible in the upper air. It does not increase wind speed.

xs: The statement that is NOT correct: friction **increases the speed of surface winds** — option **(2)**.
**Friction slows surface winds**; it is **stronger over land** and **negligible in the upper air** — so options (1), (3), (4) are true.
xa: **Coriolis force** modifies wind **direction**; **friction** modifies wind **speed**.
With no friction aloft, the **geostrophic wind** blows **parallel to isobars**.
**Pressure gradient** sets **wind speed**; air moves from high to low pressure.

16.s: When does a geostrophic wind develop?
o: Coriolis force is absent and air moves vertically
Friction alone drives air parallel to the equator
Pressure gradient force and Coriolis force balance each other, with no frictional effect
Pressure gradient force becomes zero near the poles
16.x: A geostrophic wind is an upper-air wind blowing parallel to isobars when the pressure gradient force and Coriolis force are balanced and friction is negligible.

xs: A **geostrophic wind** forms when the **pressure gradient force and Coriolis force balance**, with **no friction** — option **(3)**.

The Coriolis force is not absent — it is one of the two balancing forces.
xa: **Coriolis force** is caused by the **rotation of the Earth**; deflects **right in NH, left in SH** (**Ferrel's law**).
Coriolis is **zero at the equator**, **maximum at the poles**.
**Friction** slows surface winds, more over **land**.

o: The Coriolis force is zero or negligible
Friction over the ocean is very high
Trade winds are absent throughout the year
16.x: The Coriolis force, caused by the Earth's rotation, is zero at the equator and maximum at the poles, so the rotation needed for a cyclone cannot develop within about 5° latitude. Equatorial seas are warm, not cold; friction is low over the ocean, not high; and the trade winds do blow towards the equatorial low, so the other options are wrong.

xs: Near the equator **the Coriolis force is zero or negligible** — option **(2)**.
The **Coriolis force** is **zero at the equator** and **maximum at the poles**, so cyclones form only beyond **5°** latitude.
xa: Coriolis force is caused by the **rotation of the Earth** and deflects winds **right in NH, left in SH** (**Ferrel's law**).
It is **directly proportional to wind speed**.
**Trade winds** push tropical cyclones **westward** to east coasts; **westerlies** turn mature cyclones **north-east**.

16.s: Which of the following correctly represents the direction of the trade winds?
