20.s: What is a "biome"
o: A large naturally occurring community of flora and fauna occupying a major habitat
An endemic species with predatory nature
20.src: APPSC Group-III Panchayat Secretary Mains Paper-I General St
20.x: A biome is a large naturally occurring community of flora and fauna occupying a major habitat; it is not a species or an enzyme.

20.s: The Alpine vegetation in the western Himalayas is found only up to a height of 3000 metres, while in the eastern Himalayas it is found up to a height of 4000 metres. The reason for this variation in the same mountain range is that
o: eastern Himalayas are higher than western Himalayas
eastern Himalayas are nearer to the Equator and sea coast than western Himalayas
eastern Himalayas get more monsoon rainfall than the western Himalayas
eastern Himalayan rocks are more fertile than the western Himalayan rocks
20.x: The Eastern Himalaya is nearer the Equator and the sea (Bay of Bengal moisture), so it is warmer and the alpine/tree line stands higher (about 4,000 m) than in the Western Himalaya (3,000 m). Height or rock fertility do not explain it.

20.s: Tundra is usually a wet place because
20.src: APPSC Forest Section Officer General Studies & Mental Abilit
20.at: the low temperatures cause evaporation of water to be slow
20.x: The tundra stays wet because the low temperatures keep evaporation slow, and the permafrost below stops melt-water draining away.

20.s: To which country is the flightless bird 'kiwi' at present confined?
20.x: The kiwi is a flightless bird found only in New Zealand.

20.s:
Which of the following statements about the Equatorial region are correct?

I. It is a megathermal region.

II. It is a sclerophyll region.

III. It is a region of high development.

IV. It is a region of aerial streamlets.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
20.x: The equatorial region is megathermal (hot all year) and its multi-layered forest with climbers and epiphytes has 'aerial streamlets' – I and IV. It is not a sclerophyll (Mediterranean) region nor one of high development.

20.s: In 2019, which of the following rainforests were devastated by fire?
20.src: APPSC Assistant Chemist (AP Ground Water Service, AP Insuran
20.x: In 2019 Brazil's Amazon rainforest suffered record fires (INPE recorded a sharp rise, Aug 2019).

20.s: Identify the incorrect statement:
o: Taiga is the largest land biome in the world
This cold biome stretches across the northern portion of North America, Europe and Asia
Within this biome, there is a narrow range of temperatures between the winter and summer seasons
Precipitation in this biome is moderately high throughout the year with snow occurring during the winter months
20.x: The taiga has a very wide (not narrow) range between its long severe winter and short summer; it is the largest land biome across N America, Europe and Asia with moderate precipitation and winter snow.

20.s: Which forest type is characterized by trees that shed their leaves during the winter and hot summer months ?
20.x: Deciduous forests are made of trees that shed their leaves in the dry winter and hot summer season to save water.

20.s: Forests that are located in mid latitude areas between tropics and polar region
20.x: Temperate deciduous forests lie in the mid latitudes between the tropics and the polar regions (APPSC G2 Mains 2025).

20.s: "Leaf litter decomposes faster than in any other biome and as a result the soil surface is often almost bare. Apart from trees, the vegetation is largely composed of plant forms that reach up into the canopy vicariously, by climbing the trees or growing as epiphytes, rooted on the upper branches of trees." This is the most likely description of
20.x: Fastest litter decomposition, bare forest floor, and climbers and epiphytes reaching the canopy describe the tropical rain forest.

20.s: The maximum biodiversity is found in –

20.x: The tropical rain forest has the largest biodiversity of all biomes (over half of known species), thanks to heat and rain all year.

20.s:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as

slope angle, slope aspect and relative relief.

20.s: Which one of the following statements regarding temperate coniferous forest biome is not correct?
o: They are characterised by very little undergrowth.
They have a growing period of 50 to 100 days in a year.
There is low variation in annual temperature.
There is high range in spatial distribution of annual precipitation.
20.x: Coniferous (taiga) forests have a very high annual temperature range, so 'low variation in annual temperature' is the wrong statement; little undergrowth and a short 50–100 day growing season are true.

20.s: Spruce and cedar are tree varieties of
20.x: Spruce and cedar are needle-leaved conifers of the temperate (coniferous) forest; the temperate deciduous forest is broadleaf.

20.s: In dry regions, the leaf size of a tree becomes smaller. It is so to
20.x: Small leaves in dry regions cut water loss by transpiration.

20.s: Why do trees shed their leaves in the winter season?
o: To rest before the summer growth
To escape being eaten by animals
20.x: Trees shed leaves in winter (or the dry season) to conserve water by cutting transpiration when roots cannot draw water.

20.s: The evergreen rainforests are found in :
20.x: Evergreen tropical rainforests are found in Brazil (Amazon); Canada and France have temperate forests and Australia mostly dry lands.

20.s: Taiga forests are characteristics of –
20.x: Taiga (boreal coniferous) forest is the northernmost biome of the temperate region (cool temperate continental).

20.s: In which of the following countries of Africa, dense, hot and humid forest are found?
20.x: Ivory Coast on the Gulf of Guinea has dense hot humid forest; Kenya, Zimbabwe and South Africa are savanna or temperate.

20.s: What is a biome?
o: A transition zone between two adjacent ecosystems
An artificial ecosystem maintained only by human beings
A small community containing only one species
A large natural community of flora and fauna over a major habitat, shaped mainly by climate
20.x: A biome is a large natural community of flora and fauna occupying a major habitat and shaped by climate. It contains many habitats.
20.tq: Distinguish the definition of a biome from community, ecosystem and ecotone.
xs: A **biome** is a **large natural community of flora and fauna** over a **major habitat**, **shaped by climate** — option **(4)**.
It **contains many habitats**, so it is not a single-species community or a transition zone; human-made units are **anthromes**.
xa: **Anthromes**: ecological units shaped by **sustained human use** (croplands, villages, cities).
**Taiga** is the **largest land biome**.
**Tree line**: beyond it trees cannot grow (APPSC GS **2019**).

20.s: Anthropogenic biomes, also called anthromes, are ecological units shaped by which of the following?
o: Sustained human use such as croplands, villages and cities
20.x: Anthropogenic biomes are ecological units shaped by sustained human use and include croplands, villages and cities.
20.tq: Apply the definition to examples of human-shaped ecological units.
xs: **Anthromes** (anthropogenic biomes) are shaped by **sustained human use** — **croplands, villages, cities** — option **(1)**.
Natural biomes, by contrast, are shaped by **climate**.
xa: A **biome** contains many habitats.
**Climograph**: monthly temperature (line) + rainfall (bars).
Climate = average weather over **30 years** (WMO).

20.s: The tropical monsoon region of India and South-East Asia is chiefly associated with which vegetation?
20.x: Tropical monsoon forests in India and South-East Asia include teak and sal; the trees shed their leaves during the dry season.
20.tq: Match the climatic region with its representative vegetation.
xs: Tropical monsoon forests have **teak and sal** — option **(1)**.
Trees **shed leaves in the dry season**; rainfall **700-2,000 mm**.
**Spruce and fir** belong to the **taiga**; **mosses and lichens** to the **tundra**; **oak and maple** to temperate deciduous forests.
xa: Region: **India, SE Asia, N Australia**; seasonal wind reversal, summer rain.
AP is Koeppen **Aw** (tropical wet and dry).
Temperate deciduous trees (oak, beech, maple, birch) shed leaves in **autumn**.

20.s: What does the vegetation of the tundra mainly consist of?
20.x: Tundra has permafrost, mosses and lichens, and generally no trees.
xa: Tundra lies on **Arctic coasts** of N America and Eurasia; **alpine tundra** above the tree line.
Fauna: **reindeer, arctic fox, musk-ox**.
Peoples: **Inuit** (Canada, Alaska, Greenland), **Sami** (Scandinavia).

20.s: Tropical rainforests receive annual rainfall of more than how much?
20.x: Tropical rainforests receive over 200 cm of rain a year and stay hot and humid throughout.
n: Tropical rainforests receive more than 200 cm of rainfall. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 29-31]
Tropical rainforests have hot and humid conditions. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 29-31]
xa: They have **nutrient-poor soil** and **rapid decomposition**.
Found in the **Amazon Basin**, **Congo Basin**, **Indonesia**, **SE Asia**.

20.s: Alpine tundra is generally found in which situation?
o: In the humid equatorial belt below 10° latitude
Above the tree line in mountains such as the Himalayas, Andes and Alps
Below the tree line in tropical lowlands
20.x: Alpine tundra occurs above the tree line in high mountain systems such as the Himalayas, Andes and Alps.
20.tq: Apply the definition of alpine tundra to altitude and location.
xs: **Alpine tundra** is found **above the tree line** in the **Himalayas, Andes and Alps** — option **(2)**.
The **tree line** is where trees cannot grow, so alpine tundra cannot be below it or in equatorial lowlands.
xa: Arctic tundra: **Arctic coasts** of N America and Eurasia; **permafrost**.
Tree line asked in APPSC GS **2019**.
Koeppen **E** (polar): warmest month below **10 degC** — **ET** tundra, **EF** ice cap.

20.s: Which of the following pairs about tropical rainforests is correctly matched?
20.x: Decomposition in tropical rainforests is rapid. They also have a multilayered canopy and many climbers and epiphytes.
n: Tropical rainforests have a multilayered canopy. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 29-31]
Tropical rainforests contain climbers and epiphytes. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 29-31]
Tropical rainforests have rapid decomposition. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 29-31]
xa: Soil is **nutrient-poor** despite dense growth.
Trees: **broadleaf evergreen** hardwoods (**mahogany, ebony**).
Rainforests hold **over half** of all known species.

20.s: Which biome is often described as the world's largest terrestrial biome?
20.x: The taiga or boreal forest is often called the largest land biome.
n: The highest percentage of the world’s forest area by type is represented by temperate coniferous forests. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 29-31]
Tropical rainforests are also called Selva forests. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 29-31]
Tropical rainforests have broadleaf evergreen trees. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 29-31]
Mangrove forests are also called tidal forests. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 29-31]
Mangrove forests occur in coastal, saline, tidal environments. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 29-31]
Mangrove forests contain salt-tolerant trees. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 29-31]
Mangrove forests occur in coastal tropical regions. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 29-31]
xa: Mangroves have **salt-tolerant trees** with **pneumatophores**.
Taiga = **needle-leaved evergreen softwood** trees of **conical shape**.
Rainforests: **more than 200 cm** rainfall, **multilayered canopy**.

20.s: Tropical deciduous trees shed their leaves during which period?
20.x: Tropical deciduous trees shed leaves in the dry season to save water. Temperate deciduous trees shed in autumn.
20.tq: Discriminate tropical from temperate deciduous.
n: Tropical deciduous trees shed their leaves during the dry season. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 29-31]
xs: Tropical deciduous trees shed leaves in **the dry season** — option **(4)** is correct.
Tropical deciduous (**monsoon**) forests get **seasonal rainfall** of **100–200 cm** and shed leaves in the **dry season**.
⚠ **Temperate deciduous** trees shed leaves in **autumn**.
xa: Tropical monsoon: **seasonal wind reversal**, **summer rain**.
Trees: **teak, sal**.
Tropical rainforests are **evergreen** (more than **200 cm** rain).

20.s: Which of the following group consists entirely of wildlife of polar or tundra regions?
20.x: Krill, seals and walruses are all polar animals. Jackals and scorpions are desert animals, and beavers and lynxes live in forests.
20.tq: Recall the habitat of each animal.
n: Krill are wildlife of polar or tundra regions. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 31-33]
Seals are wildlife of polar or tundra regions. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 31-33]
Walruses are wildlife of polar or tundra regions. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 31-33]
Badgers are wildlife of temperate forests and grasslands. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 31-33]
Raccoons are wildlife of temperate forests and grasslands. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 31-33]
Koalas are wildlife of Australia's temperate forests and grasslands. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 31-33]
Lynxes are wildlife of boreal or taiga forests. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 31-33]
xs: **Krill, Seals and Walruses** are all polar/tundra wildlife — option **(4)** is correct.
**Jackals, lizards, scorpions** = **deserts/arid lands**.
**Badgers, raccoons, koalas** = **temperate**; **beavers, lynxes, wolverines** = **boreal/taiga**.
xa: Polar list also: **polar bears, penguins, musk oxen**.
**Mountains:** **snow leopards, yaks, pandas**, **condors**.
Tundra: **permafrost**, no trees; mosses, **lichens**.

20.s: Which one of the following statements about the taiga biome is NOT correct?
o: It is the largest land biome.
It has the highest productivity of all forests.
It has a wide range of temperature between winter and summer.
20.x: Taiga is the largest land biome, has a wide seasonal temperature range and moderate precipitation, but it has the lowest productivity of all forests.
20.tq: Find the statement that reverses a specific comparison.
xs: "**Highest productivity of all forests**" is wrong — option **(3)**; the taiga has the **lowest productivity** of all forests.
The rest are correct: the taiga is the **largest land biome**, with **moderate precipitation** and a **wide** winter-summer temperature range.
xa: ⚠ "Narrow range" was the incorrect statement in APPSC G1 **2023, 2024**.
Taiga soils: acidic **podzol**; trees: **spruce, fir, pine**.
**Yakuts** (Siberia) live in the taiga/Arctic.

20.s: Which one of the following statements about savanna vegetation is correct?
o: It consists exclusively of mosses and lichens over permafrost.
It is dominated by spruce, fir and pine in acidic podzol soils.
It includes elephant grass, guinea grass, baobab and acacia, and is naturally fire-prone.
It is composed mainly of olives and citrus receiving winter rain.
20.x: Savanna vegetation includes tall grasses such as elephant and guinea grass, along with baobab and acacia; it is naturally prone to fire.
20.tq: Use the vegetation list and ecological adaptation to identify the savanna.
xs: Savanna has **elephant grass, guinea grass, baobab and acacia** and is **naturally fire-prone** — option **(3)**.
Mosses over permafrost = **tundra**; spruce/fir in podzol = **taiga**; olives and citrus = **Mediterranean**.
xa: Savanna fauna: **wildebeest, zebra, giraffe**.
Climate: **wet summer, dry winter**; tall grass with scattered trees.
**Masai** (Kenya, Tanzania) are savanna herders.

20.s: Siberia, Canada and Scandinavia are covered mainly by which forest type?
20.x: Siberia, Canada and Scandinavia carry the taiga (boreal forest).
n: The Congo Basin is the second-largest tropical rainforest. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 29-31]

Temperate coniferous forests are also called boreal forests. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 29-31]
Temperate coniferous forests occur in Canada. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 29-31]
Temperate coniferous forests occur in Scandinavia. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 29-31]
Temperate coniferous forests occur in Siberia. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 29-31]

Temperate deciduous forests occur in Western Europe. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 29-31]
Mediterranean forests occur in Mediterranean lands. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 29-31]

xa: Mediterranean forests also in **California**, **Central Chile**, **SW Australia**, **Cape Province**.
**Mangroves** (tidal forests): **Sundarbans** and coastal tropics.

20.s: The taiga (boreal) biome is associated with which soil?
20.x: The taiga's evergreen conifers grow on acidic podzol soils.
xa: **Taiga is the largest land biome**; it has the **lowest productivity** of all forests.

20.s: The tree line is the altitude or latitude beyond which what happens?

xa: Above it lies **alpine tundra** — in the **Himalayas, Andes, Alps**.

20.s: What are tropical deciduous forests, which receive 100–200 cm of seasonal rain, also called?

xa: Trees **shed leaves** in the **dry season**.

23.s:

23.s: At which Temperature is the density of water noted as Maximum?
23.x: Water is densest at 4°C (anomalous behaviour); at 0°C it freezes into lighter ice.

23.s: The surface of a lake is frozen in severe winter, but the water at its bottom is still liquid. What is the reason?

Since the surface of the lake is at the same temperature as the air, no heat is lost.
The density of water is maximum at 4°c.
None of the statements (a), (b) and (c) given is correct.
23.x: As a lake cools, water at 4°C – the densest – sinks to the bottom and stays liquid while lighter colder water freezes at the top (ice insulation only helps).

23.s: An egg sinks in tap water but floats in a concentrated salt solution, because
o: the egg absorbs salt from the solution and expands
albumin dissolves in salt and the egg becomes lighter
the density of the salt solution exceeds the density of the egg
tap water has higher surface tension
23.x: Dissolved salt raises the density of the water; once the solution is denser than the egg, the egg floats.

23.s: Which one of the following denotes water salinity gradient?
23.x: The halocline is the layer of rapid salinity change with depth – the salinity gradient.

23.x: The halocline is the zone of sharp salinity change with depth; the thermocline is for temperature and the pycnocline for density.

23.s:

o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
23.x: Dissolved salts make sea water denser, giving more buoyancy, so swimming is easier: R correctly explains A.

23.s: On what does the density of ocean water mainly depend?

23.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the density of ocean water?
o: Deep ocean water is generally colder than surface water.
Deep ocean water is generally denser than surface water.
Lower temperature generally decreases the density of seawater.
Cold water sinks and fills the deep ocean.
23.x: Lower temperature increases, not decreases, the density of seawater; that is why cold, dense water sinks to the deep ocean.
n: Deep ocean water is colder than surface ocean water. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Deep ocean water is denser than surface ocean water. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Lower temperature generally produces higher density. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Surface ocean water is relatively warm. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Surface ocean water is less dense than deep ocean water. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]

23.s:
Consider the following statements:

23.x: Water is densest at 4°C, so this water sinks and the lake freezes at the top while the bottom stays liquid. Only statement 1 is correct.

23.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about oceanic clines?
o: A thermocline marks a rapid change in temperature.
A halocline marks a rapid change in salinity.
Clines promote vertical mixing of water.
A chemocline marks a rapid change in chemical characteristics.
23.x: Clines mark sharp vertical changes and act as barriers to vertical mixing; they do not promote it.
xa: **Pycnocline** = rapid change in **density**.
Density rises as **temperature falls** and **salinity rises**.

23.s: What is the ocean layer in which density increases rapidly with depth called?
23.x: Density rises sharply across the pycnocline, which therefore acts as a barrier to vertical mixing.
n: A pycnocline is a density-gradient layer. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
A pycnocline drives deep-ocean circulation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
xa: The pycnocline **drives deep-ocean circulation**.
Density rises as **temperature falls** and **salinity rises**; pressure (depth) also raises it.
**Cold polar water sinks** and creeps towards the **equator**.

23.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Thermocline – Rapid salinity change with depth
Halocline – Rapid density change with depth
Pycnocline – Rapid density change with depth
Isohalines – Rapid temperature change with depth
23.x: The pycnocline is a zone of rapid density change with depth; the thermocline marks temperature change, the halocline salinity change, and isohalines join places of equal salinity.
n: A thermocline indicates rapid temperature change with depth. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
A halocline indicates rapid salinity change with depth. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
A pycnocline indicates rapid density change with depth. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Isohalines represent salinity on maps. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
xa: Prefixes: **"thermo"** = temperature, **"halo"** = salt, **"pycno"** = density.
**Chemocline** = chemistry layer, typical of **meromictic** basins like the **Black Sea**.
Each cline is a **barrier to vertical mixing**.
⚠ **Halocline** = salinity; **pycnocline** = density.

23.s: When does the density of ocean water increase?
23.x: Density rises as temperature falls, as salinity rises and as pressure increases with depth.
xa: **Cold polar water sinks** and creeps towards the **equator**.
**Pycnocline** = zone of rapid density change.

23.s: The chemocline, a layer of rapid chemical change with depth, is a notable feature of which sea?
23.x: The Black Sea is meromictic: its layers rarely mix, and a chemocline separates oxygen-rich water from hydrogen-sulphide water.

23.s:
Consider the following statements about the density of ocean water:

2. Density rises as salinity falls.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
23.x: Density rises with pressure, falling temperature and rising salinity; it does not rise when salinity falls.

23.s: With regard to energy received from Sun, Oceans act as?

23.src: APPSC Forest Beat Officer & Assistant Beat Officer General S

Its tidal potential is ~**7,000 MW**, among the world's most significant.
**Gulf of Kutch** has **5-8 m**; the **Sundarbans** ~**5 m**; at **Chandipur** the sea recedes **several km** at low tide.
xa: **Bay of Fundy** (Canada) has the **world's greatest tidal range**.
Tidal energy: **tidal range** (barrage across an estuary) vs **tidal stream** (underwater turbines).
Bulges are higher over **wide continental shelves** — as in the Gujarat gulfs.

24.s: Where is the world's greatest tidal range found?
24.x: The Bay of Fundy in Canada is known for the world's greatest tidal range.
24.tq: Test the superlative location directly while using other major sites as distractors.
xs: The **Bay of Fundy** in **Canada** has the **world's greatest tidal range** — option **(1)**.
The Indian sites are smaller: **Gulf of Khambhat 5-10 m**, **Gulf of Kutch 5-8 m**, **Sundarbans ~5 m**.
xa: **Gulf of Khambhat** potential ~**7,000 MW** of tidal power.
**Chandipur (Odisha)**: sea recedes **several km** at low tide.
**Spring tides** (new and full moon) give the **highest range**; **neap tides** the lowest.

24.s: Gulfs that get the highest tides generally have:
24.x: Funnelling in gulfs with wide fronts and narrow rears raises the highest tides, as in the Gulf of Khambhat.

24.s: What is producing electricity with underwater turbines placed in tidal flows called?
24.x: Tidal stream uses underwater turbines; tidal range uses a barrage across an estuary.

24.s: Which of the following pairs (place – tidal feature) is correctly matched?
o: Gulf of Kutch – tidal range of 5–8 m
24.x: The Gulf of Kutch has a 5–8 m range. The Bay of Fundy is in Canada with the world's greatest range, Chandipur is where the sea recedes far, and the Sundarbans range is about 5 m.

24.s: In which state is Chandipur, where the sea recedes a few kilometres from the shore at ebb tide, located?
24.x: Chandipur on the Odisha coast is known for the sea receding a few km at low tide and coming back at high tide.

24.s: At which of the following places can one walk on the sea floor when the sea recedes several kilometres at low tide?
24.x: At Chandipur (Odisha) the sea recedes a few kilometres at ebb tide, exposing the sea floor.

24.s: What is the estimated tidal power potential of the Gulf of Khambhat, India's main tidal-energy area?
24.x: The Gulf of Khambhat (Cambay), with a tidal range of 5-10 m, has an estimated potential of about 7,000 MW.

24.s:
Which among the following statements about the North Atlantic Drift is/are correct?

I. It keeps the West Coast of Northern Europe ice free.

II. It is responsible for the warm air mass which interacts with the cold air mass from the Polar region and causes rainfall in Western Europe.

III. It meets the Labrador current near Vancouver island and causes dense fog.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
24.x: The North Atlantic Drift keeps NW Europe's ports ice-free (I) and its warm air meeting polar air brings rain to Western Europe (II). The Labrador meets the Gulf Stream at the Grand Banks off Newfoundland, not near Vancouver Island (III false).

24.s: Where are the regions where fish are found in the greatest abundance formed?
o: Where warm and cold currents meet
Where a continent touches the edge of an ocean
24.x: The best fishing grounds form where warm and cold currents meet, as mixing supports plankton.

24.s: The world's large fishing grounds are found at the junction of
24.x: Large fishing grounds such as the Grand Banks lie where warm and cold currents meet.

24.s: The most important fishing grounds of the world are found in the regions where:
o: warm and cold atmospheric currents meet
rivers drain out large amounts of fresh water into the sea
warm and cold oceanic currents meet
24.x: The most important fishing grounds lie where warm and cold oceanic currents meet (seas round Japan, east coast of North America).

24.s: The most important fishing grounds of the world are found in the regions where:
o: Warm and cold atmospheric currents meet
Rivers drain out large amounts of fresh water into the sea
Warm and cold oceanic currents meet
24.x: The most important fishing grounds lie where warm and cold oceanic currents meet; 'atmospheric currents' is the trap.

24.s: Grand Bank is located at :
24.x: The Grand Banks lie SE of Newfoundland on the eastern coast of North America, where the Labrador meets the Gulf Stream.

24.s: The current produced by upwelling of cold water off the coast of Chile and Peru is known as
24.x: The cold Humboldt (Peru) Current, with its upwelling, flows off Chile and Peru; El Nino is a warm episode.

24.s: Coastal areas next to warm ocean currents are generally:
24.x: Warm currents warm adjacent coastal areas, while cold currents cool them.
n: Warm currents can warm adjacent coastal areas. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]
Cold currents can cool adjacent coastal areas. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]
xa: Warm currents are often from **lower latitudes**, moving **toward higher latitudes**.
Cold currents come from **higher-latitude** or cold-water regions.
Currents **redistribute heat** and **influence climate**.

24.s: Which current gives north-western Europe its mild climate and keeps ports in Norway and Murmansk ice-free?
24.x: The North Atlantic Drift, an extension of the Gulf Stream, carries warm water towards north-western Europe and helps keep its coasts mild and ports ice-free in winter.
24.tq: Match a climatic effect and location with the responsible warm current.
xs: The **North Atlantic Drift** keeps **NW Europe** mild and ports ice-free in winter, e.g. **Murmansk** — option **(1)**.
It is the warm extension of the **Gulf Stream**, which runs off the **USA east coast → NW Europe**.
**California**, **Oyashio** and **Benguela** are all **cold** currents — they cannot warm Europe.
xa: The **Norwegian** current is also a **warm** North Atlantic current.
The North Atlantic Drift forms the **northern** boundary of the **Sargasso Sea**.
North Atlantic gyre: **N. Equatorial - Gulf Stream - N. Atlantic Drift - Canary**.

24.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the meeting of warm and cold ocean currents?
o: The rich fishing grounds off Japan form where the Kuroshio meets the Benguela.
The Gulf Stream meets the Labrador Current at the Grand Banks near Newfoundland.
Fog forms frequently near Newfoundland where warm and cold currents meet.
The Benguela is a South Atlantic current.
24.x: Off Japan the Kuroshio meets the Oyashio; the Benguela is a South Atlantic current.

24.s: The Namib and Kalahari deserts are associated with which ocean current?
24.x: The Namib and Kalahari are associated with the Benguela; the Atacama goes with the Humboldt and the Sonoran with the California Current.
xa: Cold currents along **west coasts** chill and dry coastal lands → **deserts**.
**Somalia** fishery — **Findlater** upwelling.
**El Nino**: warm water replaces the cold Peruvian current, **suppressing upwelling** → **fewer phytoplankton**.

24.s: Which of the following mainly helps form arid desert climates on west coasts?
24.x: Cold currents cool the coast and suppress convection, helping make west-coast deserts.
n: Warm currents warm adjoining coastal air. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cold currents cool adjoining coasts. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cold currents can suppress convection. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cold currents combined with subtropical highs are often associated with arid west-coast climates. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xa: Desert examples: **Atacama** (Humboldt), **Namib/Kalahari** (Benguela), **Sonoran** (California).
**North Atlantic Drift** keeps **NW Europe** mild and ports like **Murmansk** ice-free.
Warm currents **increase moisture availability**.

24.s: Along the coasts of which countries is upwelling of cold, nutrient-rich water particularly important for fisheries?
24.x: Cold, nutrient-rich upwelling supports fisheries along Peru and near Somalia, where the Somali (Findlater) current system is involved.
xa: Where warm and cold currents meet, **plankton flourishes** → fishing grounds (Grand Banks; off **Japan**, Kuroshio + Oyashio).
The Findlater upwelling zone is **small**, so its effect on the Indian monsoon is **limited** (unlike the **IOD**).
During **El Nino** upwelling off Peru is **suppressed** → **fewer phytoplankton**; **La Nina** brings strong upwelling.

24.s: The Atacama Desert is associated with which cold current?
24.x: The Humboldt helps form the Atacama; the Benguela the Namib and Kalahari, and the California the Sonoran.

24.s: The Sonoran Desert is associated with which cold current?
24.x: The cold California current helps form the Sonoran Desert.

24.s: Between which latitudes do the best fishing grounds, where warm and cold currents meet, mainly lie?
24.x: The best fishing grounds form where warm and cold currents meet, mainly at 40°–60°.

24.s: What explains the eastward flow of the equatorial counter-current?
o: The Earth's rotation on its axis
Convergence of the two equatorial currents
Occurrence of the belt of calm near the equator
24.x: The westward North and South Equatorial Currents pile up water in the west; this water flows back eastward between them as the Equatorial Counter Current.

24.s: What explains the eastward flow of the equatorial counter-current?
o: The Earth's rotation on its axis
Convergence of the two equatorial currents
Occurrence of the Belt of Calm near the equator
24.x: The convergence of the two westward equatorial currents piles up water in the west, which returns eastward as the counter current – not Earth's rotation.

24.s: Which one among the following is not a cause of generation of ocean currents?
o: Shape and configuration of the coastlines.
24.x: Planetary winds, temperature (density) differences and coastline shape drive or steer currents; the Earth's revolution round the Sun does not.

24.s:
Consider the following statements.

I. Ocean currents are large mass of surface water that circulate in regular patterns around the oceans.

II. The planetary winds are probably the dominant influence on the flow of ocean currents.

III. The water of high salinity are denser than the water of low salinity.

IV. A landmass always obstructs and diverts an ocean current.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
24.x: Currents are surface water circulating in regular patterns (I), driven mainly by planetary winds (II), and saltier water is denser (III). A landmass deflects but does not always obstruct a current, so IV is false.

24.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Ocean currents are the slow-surface movement of water in the ocean.
2. Ocean currents assist in maintaining the Earth's heat balance
3. Ocean currents are set in motion primarily by prevailing winds
4. Ocean currents are affected by the configuration of the ocean. Which of these statements are correct?
24.x: Currents are slow surface movements (1), help keep the heat balance (2), are set in motion mainly by prevailing winds (3) and are affected by the ocean's configuration (4): all four.

24.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Cold polar water sinks and creeps towards the equator.
2. Differences in density drive deep ocean currents.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
24.x: Denser water sinks and lighter water rises; this drives deep currents, as cold polar water sinks and creeps towards the equator.

24.s: Which ocean-water phenomenon involves horizontal movement and has major impacts on climate, fisheries and navigation?
24.x: Ocean currents are horizontal movements that affect climate, fisheries and navigation. Tides are vertical changes in level.
n: Ocean currents involve horizontal movement of water. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]
Ocean currents affect climate, fisheries, and navigation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]
Ocean currents produce horizontal water movement. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]
Ocean currents affect climate, fisheries, and navigation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]
xs: **Ocean currents** — option **(2)** is correct.
Currents are **continuous directed**, **horizontal movement** of water affecting **climate, fisheries and navigation**.
**Tides** are **vertical, periodic** changes in water level; **waves** are **oscillatory** movements.
xa: Current drivers: **winds**, **density differences**, **Coriolis force**, **pressure differences**.
Currents are **relatively continuous**; tides **highly periodic**; waves **variable**.
**Tsunamis** have **different causes** from wind-driven waves.

24.s: Which of the following pairs (movement of ocean water – its nature) is correctly matched?
o: Tides – Periodic rise and fall of sea level caused mainly by the Moon and the Sun
Currents – Oscillatory movement of water with no forward flow
Waves – Continuous directed flow of water over long distances
24.x: Tides are the periodic rise and fall of sea level caused mainly by the gravity of the Moon and the Sun (and can be harnessed as tidal energy). Currents are a continuous directed flow of water, waves are an oscillatory movement, and irregular weather-driven surges are storm surges, not tides.
n: Tides contribute to tidal energy. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]

24.s: Which factor deflects ocean currents to the right in the Northern Hemisphere?
24.x: The Coriolis effect deflects currents to the right in the Northern Hemisphere; westerlies drive mid-latitude currents, coastlines redirect them and floor relief steers them.
n: Westerlies drive mid-latitude currents. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
The Coriolis effect deflects ocean currents. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Coastline configuration deflects currents. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Ocean-floor relief modifies current direction. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
xa: **Trade winds** drive **major surface currents** (equatorial currents westward).
**Deep-ocean currents** are driven by **density differences** from **temperature and salinity**.
**Equatorial Counter Current** flows **west to east** through the **doldrums**.

24.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about ocean currents?
o: Solar heating contributes to their movement.
Density differences have no role in their movement.
The Coriolis force deflects them to the right in the Northern Hemisphere.
24.x: Density differences, along with solar heating, wind, gravity and the Coriolis force, do influence ocean currents.
xa: An ocean current = a **steady volume of water** moving along a **set path**.
**Trade winds** drive equatorial currents **westward**; **westerlies** drive drifts **eastward**.
**Gyres** form from winds, **Coriolis force** and **land barriers**.

24.s: What does solar heating do to ocean water near the equator?
o: Expand, creating a slight slope down which water flows
Flow towards the equator from the poles
24.x: Solar heating expands equatorial water, creating a slight surface slope down which gravity moves water.
xa: **Density differences**: saltier, colder water is **denser → sinks**; lighter water rises → **thermohaline** circulation.
Warm currents move from the **equator towards the poles** along the surface.
**Coriolis force** deflects currents **right in the N hemisphere**, **left in the S**.

24.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about density-driven ocean circulation?
o: Density differences help drive deep thermohaline circulation.
Saltier water is denser than less salty water.
Cold water sinking at the poles moves rapidly towards the equator.
24.x: Cold water that sinks at the poles moves slowly, not rapidly, towards the equator.
xa: Other drivers: **solar heating, wind, gravity, Coriolis force**.
**Cold currents** move from poles towards the equator, usually along **west coasts**.
**Upwelling** brings **cold, nutrient-rich** water up — e.g. **Peru/Humboldt**, **Somalia/Findlater**.

24.s: In which direction does the Equatorial Counter Current flow?
o: From south to north only in the Indian Ocean
From north to south along the western coasts of continents
From east to west between the polar currents
From west to east between the North and South Equatorial Currents
24.x: The Equatorial Counter Current flows west to east between the North and South Equatorial Currents. It returns water piled up in the west through the calm doldrums belt.
24.tq: Identify the current by its position and direction rather than by its name alone.
xs: The **Equatorial Counter Current** flows **west to east** between the **North and South Equatorial Currents** — option **(4)**.
**Trade winds** pile water on the **western side**; it flows back east through the calm **doldrums** belt.
The equatorial currents themselves flow **westward**; west-coast equatorward flows are **cold currents**.
xa: **Trade winds** → equatorial currents westward; **westerlies** → drifts eastward.
North Atlantic gyre: **N. Equatorial - Gulf Stream - N. Atlantic Drift - Canary**.
Gyres run **clockwise** in the Northern Hemisphere, **anticlockwise** in the Southern.

24.s:
Assertion (A): Ocean currents influence climate.
Reason (R): Ocean currents redistribute heat.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
24.x: Both are true and R explains A: by carrying heat from low to high latitudes, currents warm or cool the coasts they pass.
24.tq: Check whether R is the cause of A.
n: Ocean currents redistribute heat. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Ocean currents influence climate. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
Ocean currents **redistribute heat** and thereby **influence climate**.
Warm currents can **warm** and cold currents **cool** **adjacent coastal areas**.
xa: Warm currents move **toward higher latitudes**; cold currents **toward lower latitudes**.
Warm currents usually run along **east coasts**; cold along **west coasts**.
Where **warm + cold currents meet**, **plankton** flourishes and **fog** forms (e.g. **Newfoundland**).

24.s: Which planetary winds primarily drive the equatorial ocean currents westward?
24.x: Trade winds push surface water westward and drive the equatorial currents. Westerlies generally drive oceanic drifts eastward.
24.tq: Use the wind-direction relationship to distinguish trade winds from westerlies.
xs: **Trade winds** push the equatorial currents **westward** — option **(2)**.
**Westerlies** drive the oceanic **drifts eastward**, the opposite direction.
**Monsoon winds** reverse the **North Indian Ocean** currents seasonally; they are not the planetary driver of equatorial currents.
xa: Water piled up on the **western side** by trades flows back east as the **Equatorial Counter Current** through the **doldrums**.
**Wind friction** pushes surface water — the basis of wind-driven currents.
ENSO: during **La Nina** trade winds **strengthen**; during **El Nino** they **weaken or reverse**.

24.s: What do cold, salty waters that sink at the poles and move slowly towards the equator form?
24.x: Temperature and salinity differences make cold, salty polar water sink and move slowly to the equator: the thermohaline circulation.

24.s: In the Southern Hemisphere, in which direction does the Coriolis force deflect ocean currents?
24.x: The Coriolis force deflects currents to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern.

24.s: The Sargasso Sea is characterized by –
24.x: The Sargasso Sea is named after the floating Sargassum weed that covers it – typical marine vegetation.

24.s: Where is Sargasso sea situated?
24.x: The Sargasso Sea lies in the North Atlantic, bounded by currents instead of land.

24.s: The Sargasso Sea is a part of the-
24.x: The Sargasso Sea is part of the North Atlantic Ocean.

24.s: Which one of the following currents does not contribute to forming a complete circle of currents in the South Atlantic Ocean:
24.x: The South Atlantic circle is South Equatorial – Brazil – West Wind Drift – Benguela; the Canary Current belongs to the North Atlantic.

24.s: Which of the following seas does not have a coastline?
24.x: The Sargasso Sea is bounded only by currents, so it has no coastline; the Black Sea, Sea of Azov and Caspian all have coasts.

24.s: Which one of the following forms the northern boundary of the Sargasso Sea?
24.x: The Sargasso Sea is bounded by the North Atlantic Drift in the north, the Gulf Stream in the west, the Canary Current in the east and the North Equatorial Current in the south.
24.tq: Test one boundary of a current-defined region.
xs: The **North Atlantic Drift** forms the **northern** boundary of the **Sargasso Sea** — option **(4)**.
Other boundaries: **Gulf Stream (W)**, **Canary Current (E)**, **North Equatorial Current (S)**.
xa: The Sargasso Sea is the only sea bounded by **currents, not land** — "sea without shores".
It is the calm centre of the **North Atlantic gyre**; calm, warm, salty, with floating **Sargassum** seaweed.
The **North Atlantic Drift** (Gulf Stream extension) keeps **NW Europe** mild and **Murmansk** ice-free.

24.s: Why is the Sargasso Sea unusual?
o: the only sea bounded by ocean currents rather than land
a sea enclosed entirely by coral reefs
the only sea located in the Southern Hemisphere
24.x: The Sargasso Sea lies in the North Atlantic and is bounded by currents rather than land. It is also calm, warm, salty and rich in floating Sargassum weed.
24.tq: Use the distinctive geographical exception in the definition.
xs: The **Sargasso Sea** is the **only sea bounded by currents rather than land** — option **(2)**.
It lies in the **North Atlantic** (Northern Hemisphere) and is full of floating **Sargassum** seaweed — so options (1) and (4) are wrong.
xa: Boundaries: **Gulf Stream (W)**, **North Atlantic Drift (N)**, **Canary (E)**, **North Equatorial Current (S)**.
It is the calm centre of the **North Atlantic gyre**; calm, **warm, salty**.
Called the **"sea without shores"**.

24.s: Which current bounds the Sargasso Sea on the east?
24.x: The Sargasso Sea is bounded by the Gulf Stream (west), North Atlantic Drift (north), Canary (east) and North Equatorial (south).

24.s: The South Pacific gyre is closed on its eastern side by which cold current?
24.x: The South Pacific gyre runs South Equatorial – East Australian – West Wind Drift – Humboldt.

24.s: In which direction do oceanic gyres circulate in the Northern Hemisphere?
o: Clockwise in summer and anticlockwise in winter
24.x: Gyres turn clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and anticlockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.
xa: **North Atlantic gyre:** N. Equatorial – **Gulf Stream** – N. Atlantic Drift – **Canary**.
**South Indian Ocean gyre:** South Equatorial → **Agulhas** → West Wind Drift → **West Australian**.
**Sargasso Sea** = calm centre of the North Atlantic gyre — "**sea without shores**".

24.s: During which months does the West India Coastal Current flow northward?
24.x: During the winter (NE) monsoon, November–February, the West India Coastal Current flows northward (poleward); in the SW monsoon it flows south.

24.s: Which one of the following factors is responsible for the change in the regular direction of the ocean currents in the Indian Ocean?
o: Indian Ocean is a land-locked ocean
Indian Ocean has greater variation in salinity
24.x: North Indian Ocean currents reverse with the monsoon winds (monsoon drift), unlike those of the other oceans.

24.s: Which one of the following factors is responsible for the change in the regular direction of the ocean currents in the Indian Ocean?
o: Indian Ocean is half an Ocean
Indian Ocean is a land-locked ocean
Indian Ocean has greater variation in salinity
24.x: North Indian Ocean currents reverse with the monsoon winds (monsoon drift), unlike those of the other oceans.

24.s: Which ocean region is unique in having currents that reverse direction seasonally with the monsoon winds?
24.x: North Indian Ocean currents reverse with the monsoon winds; the South Indian Ocean has a permanent anticlockwise gyre.

24.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about ocean circulation during the southwest monsoon season?
o: Circulation in the Arabian Sea is clockwise.
Circulation in the Bay of Bengal is clockwise.
The West India Coastal Current flows southward.
The East India Coastal Current flows southward.
24.x: During the southwest monsoon the EICC flows northward, not southward; the circulation is clockwise and the WICC flows southward.

24.s: In which direction does the West India Coastal Current flow during November–February?
24.x: The WICC flows northward (poleward) in November–February and southward during the southwest monsoon.
xa: This WICC fact was the **APPSC GS 2018** key.
The **EICC** also reverses: **northward Feb-Sep**, **southward Oct-Dec**.
North Indian Ocean: SW monsoon **clockwise**, NE monsoon **anticlockwise**.

24.s: In which sea does the Findlater Current, tied to the Somali Jet, flow?
24.x: The Findlater Current is an Arabian Sea current that reverses with the monsoon and causes upwelling off the Horn of Africa.
xa: **Somalia/Findlater** upwelling and **Peru/Humboldt** upwelling both support fisheries.
Upwelling brings **cold, nutrient-rich** water to the surface.
**NIOT** OMNI buoys feed **IOD** monitoring.

24.s: What is the direction of circulation in the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea during the north-east monsoon?
24.x: In the NE monsoon the circulation is anticlockwise; in the SW monsoon it is clockwise.

24.s: Off which coast does upwelling linked to the Findlater Current occur?
24.x: The Findlater Current (Somali Jet) reverses with the monsoon and drives upwelling off the Horn of Africa.

24.s: In which direction does the East India Coastal Current flow during the north-east (winter) monsoon?
24.x: In the NE monsoon the Bay of Bengal circulation is anticlockwise, so the EICC flows southward; in the SW monsoon it flows northward.

25.s: Which of the following Planetary climatic event is associated with El Nino?
25.src: APPSC Forest Section Officer General Studies & Mental Abilit
25.at: Heat and high rainfall lead to flooding of the coastal zone of South America, especially Peru and Ecuador and also the Pacific coast of Colombia and northern Chile
25.x: El Nino brings heat and heavy rain to the normally arid coast of Peru and Ecuador (and coastal Colombia, northern Chile), flooding it, while Indonesia and northern Australia get drought.

25.s: ____ is a climate phenomenon that occurs when a vast pool of water in the eastern tropical Pacific ocean becomes abnormally warm.
25.src: APPSC Asst. B.C. Welfare Officers, Royalty Inspector
25.x: El Nino is the abnormal warming of the eastern tropical Pacific; La Nina is the opposite, cooling phase.

25.s:
El-Nino is a complex weather system that appears once every three to seven years. Consider the following state
A. The appearance of warm currents off the Coast of Peru in the Eastern Pacific.
B. The word El-Nino means ' Christ Child ' because the current appears around Christmas in December.
C. El-Nino was one of the reasons for the deficit rainfall in India (2014).
Which of the statements given above is / are correct?
25.x: All three are correct: El Nino is a warm current off Peru in the eastern Pacific, its name means 'Christ child' because it appears around Christmas, and it contributed to India's 2014 monsoon deficit (about 12% below normal).

25.s: Which of the following statements is not correct ?
o: El Nino is an ocean current, which appears off the
El Nino weakens the Indian Monsoon
La Nina strengthens the Indian Monsoon
25.x: El Nino recurs irregularly, about every 3-7 years, not every year. The other statements are true: it is a warm current off Peru, weakens the Indian monsoon, and La Nina strengthens it.

25.s: Where does the El Nino current flow?
o: More than one of the above
25.x: El Nino is a Pacific Ocean phenomenon (off Peru and Ecuador), not an Indian Ocean or Bay of Bengal one.

25.s: El-Nino develops in the
25.x: El Nino develops in the eastern and central equatorial Pacific Ocean, off Peru and Ecuador.

25.s:
With reference to the “EL-NINO”, which of the following statement/s is/are correct?
(1) El Nino involves appearance of warm current off the coast of Peru in eastern pacific.
(2) This warm current increase the temperature of water on the Peruvian coast by 10°C there by increasing the amount of Plankton in the sea.
Select the correct answer using the code given below-
25.x: Statement 1 is right: El Nino is a warm current off Peru. Statement 2 is wrong: the warm water cuts off the cold, nutrient-rich upwelling, so plankton and the fish catch fall, not rise.

25.s: ‘El Nino’ associated with the formation of the South-West Monsoon of India is
25.x: El Nino is an abnormally warm ocean current that replaces the cold Peruvian current; it is oceanic, not an air mass, a wind or a low-pressure centre, though it affects the Indian monsoon.

25.s:
Which among the following statements characterise El Nino?

I. It occurs at irregular intervals.

II. It carries warmer water.

III. It carries less saline water.

IV. Its atmospheric equivalent is Southern oscillation.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
